articles.title: Doctor Doom Is Not a Tony Stark Variant in Avengers: Doomsday, Confirms Kevin Feige
articles.description: Kevin Feige has confirmed that Doctor Doom is not a variant of Tony Stark in Avengers: Doomsday.
articles.content:
Kevin Feige has confirmed that Doctor Doom is not a variant of Tony Stark in Avengers: Doomsday.

When speaking with Empire Magazine, Marvel Studios boss Kevin Feige debunked the popular fan theory that Doctor Doom and Tony Stark have a shared connection in the multiverse. Fans have speculated that Doom is a "variant" of Stark, since Robert Downey Jr. plays both characters. Variants are other versions of a character across the multiverse. We've seen this with the three Spider-Men, Wolverine, and Loki, so naturally, some fans thought this may all be an elaborate way to explain how Robert Downey Jr. is also playing Doom... turns out, it's not.

“Is Steve Rogers a Johnny Storm variant?" asked Feige. "People wondered, ‘Is Doom just a variant of another character? Is this just a shortcut to bringing back another character?’ The answer is no. He’s Victor Von Doom.”

As for what Doom's whole deal is, the creative team behind the film teased what kind of energy he brings and why he is the way he is. The Russo Brothers, who are directing the film, teased that Doom has lost a child, is a "victim of trauma" and has a greater ego than Thanos. They also noted that he's a pretty terrifying presence.

"Doom is a Gothic character,” said director Joe Russo. “He says, ‘Hell answers to me,’ and he’s not kidding. He’s a very powerful character with some very dark magic, and he’s not above selling his soul to get what he wants. He’s worth being scared of.”

Robert Downey Jr. also noted that he was excited to lean into being a villain this time around, and suggested that Doom's plans have a tremendous scope to them.

"I like a bit of scorched earth,” teases Downey Jr. “Whatever you think he may be entertaining, I would ten times it, and you’ll probably be closer to the ballpark."

There's still a lot that we don't know about the film, which is just a little over a month away from being released. A recent listing on the WGA's website credited Hugh Jackman and Ryan Reynolds for contributing to the film's script, which seems to suggest Wolverine and Deadpool may be in the film. Additionally, Marvel confirmed earlier this week that Scarlet Witch will also return in Avengers: Doomsday, though seemingly under the control of Doom himself.

Avengers: Doomsday hits theaters on December 18.

articles.title: The Lord of the Rings: Rings of Power Season 3 Resolves One of the Most Fascinating Mysteries From Middle-earth Lore
articles.description: Rings of Power Season 3 has revealed the true identity of Ciarán Hinds’ Dark Wizard, thereby resolving one of the biggest mysteries from J.R.R. Tolkien's Middle-earth lore.
articles.content:
Full spoilers ahead for the first four episodes of The Lord of the Rings: Rings of Power Season 3!

Prime Video has released the first four episodes of The Rings of Power Season 3, and they’re nothing if not eventful. But amid all the warring and hoarding of magical rings, there’s also a reveal that has a lot of Tolkien nerds’ heads spinning. The series has resolved what may well be the biggest lingering mystery from Tolkien’s vast Middle-earth mythology.

Read on for a full breakdown of the big reveal in Episode 3 and how it resolves a major loose end from books like The Silmarillion and Unfinished Tales of Middle-earth.

Ciarán Hinds’ Dark Wizard Revealed

Back in Season 2, viewers were introduced to a new antagonist played by Ciarán Hinds. Known as the “Dark Wizard,” this villain reigns over the cursed land of Rhûn. Gandalf (Daniel Weyman) is desperate to put a stop to this powerful foe, lest the Dark Wizard ally himself with Sauron and create a truly unstoppable army.

Though Rings of Power is set many centuries before the events of The Lord of the Rings trilogy, many of the characters are designed to evoke familiar archetypes from the movies. Once again, we have a saga crammed full of noble elves, intrepid dwarves, plucky Hobbits (or Harfoots), and morally conflicted men. But sometimes those archetypes are subverted in the end. Much like how the seemingly Aragorn-esque Halbrand (Charlie Vickers) turned out to be Sauron, the Dark Wizard isn’t who many fans assumed him to be.

Initially, Hinds’ character was speculated to be Saruman, given that he’s a dark wizard with great ambitions and a willingness to fight alongside Sauron. But that never quite made sense, as it’s not until the end of the Third Age that Saruman allows his true motivations to be known. Season 3, Episode 3 instead confirms a different fan theory, revealing the Dark Wizard to be a being known as Pallando.

Tolkien didn’t write a great deal about Pallando (we’ll get more into that shortly), but the gist is that Eru Ilúvatar (the God of this fantasy universe) originally sent five wizards to Middle-earth to aid the kingdoms of elves and men in their war against Sauron. Alongside Gandalf the Grey, there were also Saruman the White, Radagast the Brown, and the two Blue Wizards, Alatar and Pallando. Radagast became mostly distracted by his love of the wilderness and animals, and the two Blue Wizards vanished into obscurity, leaving only Gandalf and Saruman to carry on the fight into the Third Age.

The series extrapolates on this backstory by revealing Hinds to be Pallando. In a conversation with the disembodied form of Eru Ilúvatar, Gandalf learns that Pallando became corrupted by his thirst for power and murdered Alatar. That act poisoned the realm of Rhûn. Despite this, Gandalf’s mission isn’t to stop Pallando, but to appeal to his better nature and convince him to stop his army from joining Sauron. Even Dark Wizards can be redeemed, it seems.

What Did Tolkien Reveal About the Blue Wizards?

The two Blue Wizards were never a big focus of Tolkien’s writings, which perhaps explains why they’re a source of such fascination among fans. They don’t appear at all in The Hobbit or The Lord of the Rings trilogy, leaving only a handful of scattered references in posthumously published works like Unfinished Tales of Middle-earth and The Peoples of Middle-earth.

As Tolkien established, Pallando was one of five Maiar (immortal beings of the same race as Sauron himself) who were handpicked to travel from the Undying Lands to Middle-earth to help rally resistance against Sauron. Pallando and Alatar were known as the Blue Wizards (or “Ithryn Luin” in the ancient language of Sindarin) because of their distinctive sea blue robes. Originally, only Alatar, Gandalf, and Saruman were chosen for this quest, but Alatar opted to invite Pallando along, and Radagast was also added to the group for some reason.

Once in Middle-earth, the various wizards split up and picked different areas to focus on. Saruman, Alatar, and Pallando journeyed east to appeal to the Easterlings and the Haradrim. And that’s about where the latter two characters’ story ends in Tolkien’s writings. Saruman eventually returned to the West and set up shop in Isengard, but Alatar and Pallando never came with him. They just disappeared, hence why when Ian McKellen’s Gandalf mentions the Blue Wizards in 2012’s The Hobbit: An Unexpected Journey, he can’t even remember their names (technically, that was because the filmmakers didn’t have the rights to use characters from Unfinished Tales).

Tolkien himself seemed pretty pessimistic about whether the Blue Wizards ultimately succeeded in their mission. Tolkien himself seemed pretty pessimistic about whether the Blue Wizards ultimately succeeded in their mission. In a letter published after his death, Tolkien wrote, “I think that they went as emissaries to distant regions, east and south... Missionaries to enemy-occupied lands as it were. What success they had I do not know; but I fear that they failed, as Saruman did, though doubtless in different ways; and I suspect they were founders or beginners of secret cults and ‘magic’ traditions that outlasted the fall of Sauron."

This lack of textual information has only fueled speculation about the Blue Wizards over the decades, to the point where they’ve become a major source of fascination for hardcore Tolkien nerds. What actually became of Alatar and Pallando? Now we finally know.

Obviously, Rings of Power is doing a lot of embellishing to build on what little Tolkien established about these characters. Now we know that Alatar and Pallando didn’t just fail in their mission; the latter actively became the sort of threat he was designed to quash. However, the series is hinting that there may still be a redemption arc in store for Pallando. The character is currently subservient to Sauron, but we suspect that’ll change as the final seasons of the show unfold. There may still be a chance for this fallen wizard to do some good and play a part in Sauron’s downfall, even if he’s doomed to be forgotten by history.

For more on Rings of Power, check out IGN’s review of Season 3, Episodes 1-4 and learn more about the big character deaths in these episodes.

articles.title: Palantir’s Karp takes a sharp left turn, says he and the company’s products are actually ‘progressive’
articles.description: Trump donor says he privately questioned deportation tactics. Shame about the privately bit
articles.content:
With tech CEO roles, a certain level of shamelessness comes with the job description. Yet Alex Karp, head honcho of Palantir, seems set to raise the bar with a conspicuous display of political flexibility following the Democratic wave in the US midterms.

In December 2024, Karp gave $1 million to the pro-Trump super PAC MAGA Inc.

But it does not take cutting-edge AI and data analytics – in which Palantir claims to have unique power – for Karp to understand on which side his bread is buttered. The man with the distinctive verbal diarrhea is now stressing his progressive credentials – and those of Palantir's products.

The CEO told Politico that he is now open to voting for the Democrats come 2028.

"I've been a Democrat my whole life. I grew up in a far-left environment. I know more about being a progressive than almost anybody on the planet, and I absolutely believe Palantir – all of our products are essentially progressive," Karp reportedly said.

Karp's explanation for his political generosity was an apparent desire for balance.

"My giving is equal, Democrat, Republican," Karp told the publication. "I can tell you, without going into things I'm not gonna disclose, I'm very balanced, and everyone in the political arena knows it. And I'll tell you what, I'm also not the village idiot."

All of which raises the question of whether, in avoiding idiocy, it is necessary to eschew any principled stance whatsoever. If only the Germans of the Weimar Republic had thought to fund both sides. Apparently, all Europe needed was a more balanced political donations portfolio.

Such is Karp's sensitivity towards the topic that he once claimed: "I love when I'm getting yelled at in cities in Europe... Keep yelling at me... the only reason why someone's not goose-stepping between me and you is my product. Say thank you."

They have not said thank you. In fact, across Europe, governments are looking to reject Palantir, while the EU has instigated a sovereign tech and AI policy to escape the clutches of the US tech giants.

Karp has a talent for holding two seemingly contradictory positions. He has talked about the need for democratic societies to exercise hard power, and, elsewhere, about founding a company that could "power the West to its obvious innate superiority."

At the same time, he has presented Palantir as a force for peace. "We see ourselves as the pioneers of a genuine and viable antiwar movement," he wrote in his shareholder letter.

It is his company's association with a longstanding customer, the controversial US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), that has drawn the most criticism. In Minnesota earlier this year, federal immigration officers shot and killed two American citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, in incidents captured on video. It has detained US citizens, and critics argue it has shown scant regard for due process.

Karp denied that Palantir's association with ICE should reflect badly on the company.

He told CNBC: " If you are critical of ICE, you should be out there protesting for more Palantir. Our product, actually, in its core, requires people to conform with Fourth Amendment data protection."

In the Politico interview, Karp said he was "really happy to hear" President Trump, a driving force behind ICE's expansion, acknowledge after the midterm elections that ICE deportations have been too tough.

"And I'm glad he's saying in public now what I've been saying in private," Karp told the news outlet.

Karp has no shortage of public opinions on goose-stepping or innate Western superiority. Why, then, reserve his concerns about deportations for private conversations? A public intervention from a Trump donor and ICE supplier might have carried some weight.

Maybe he doesn't care so long as people are still writing about Alex Karp. But anyone who cares about more than that might feel the need to take a hot shower and scrub off the associated trauma. ®

articles.content:
Hugh Jackman and Ryan Reynolds have been credited for contributing to Avengers: Doomsday's script, all but confirming the return of Deadpool and Wolverine.

Per an update to the Writers Guild of America's website, Avengers: Doomsday has credited a handful of people for contributing to the film's script. Although the screenplay was written by Stephen McFeely and Michael Waldron, the Additional Literary Material section confirms that Eric Pearson, Chris McKenna, Erik Sommers, Jeff Loveness, Andrew Lanham, Destin Daniel Cretton, Ryan Reynolds, and Hugh Jackman also contributed to the script. These credits are for people who are not the authors of the actual film's story, but helped punch up dialogue or did a small pass on the script.

With that said, Ryan Reynolds is well-known for helping write the Deadpool films, and it would be surprising for him to have helped out on this specific script if Deadpool wasn't in it. Although Hugh Jackman doesn't have a history as a writer, he may have also helped write Wolverine's scenes, as well, given he has spent 26 years playing the character.

The characters have been repeatedly teased to return in Doomsday by both Jackman and Reynolds, with the two doing tongue-in-cheek promos at San Diego Comic-Con and D23 over the summer. However, they haven't been explicitly confirmed to appear in the film. Since Deadpool and Wolverine were huge hits and fans have hoped to see the characters in an Avengers film for years, it only makes sense for them to finally crossover into the broader MCU.

Additionally, Spider-Man: Brand New Day director Destin Daniel Cretton also got a credit for Doomsday, but it's worth remembering he also directed Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings. Shang-Chi is confirmed to appear in the upcoming ensemble film, so it's more likely that his contributions are for helping write that character. It's possible Spider-Man is in the film, but it remains unclear at the moment.

Marvel also confirmed earlier this week that another major MCU character will return in Doomsday after a four-year absence. Scarlet Witch was seen at the end of VisionQuest being abducted by Doctor Doom, following her appearance in Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness. As a result, it seems like she may be an antagonist once again, though this time under the control of another character.

articles.title: Software Samaritan revamps borked Indian certs to block smart TV ads
articles.description: A little tinkering can black hole obnoxious Samsung TV ads and some tracking, until a firmware fix ruins the fun
articles.content:
eMudhra's private key exposure has been a security disaster, but it also means that you can block those annoying ads on smart TVs if you’re so inclined.

Luckily for those with some know-how and a hatred of smart TV ads, Czech software developer Daniel Vrátil has done the work for you and published his project on GitHub for anyone who wants to take a stab at it - and do the legwork to add support for their own ad-riddled television.

Vrátil said he’d been blocking ads on his Samsung smart TV using a Pi-hole (DNS-based ad-blocking software that can run on a Raspberry Pi, for those unfamiliar), but right around the time the eMudhra certificate leak mess unfolded, he had messed something up while tinkering with his home lab and the ads were back.

First, here's a bit of background on the eMudhra mess. The company, based in India, operated a publicly trusted HTTPS certificate authority and says it has issued more than 60 million digital certificates. As we learned last month, eMudhra wasn't doing its best to keep its cryptographic keys safe: Eight intermediate CA private keys were found to be absurdly weak, with one being the number four and the others consisting of two- or three-digit numbers that could be guessed with little effort.

eMudhra has since left the CA racket, saying that it wasn’t a big deal to it since issuing certs was a small part of its business. The company has blamed a bad software script put in place to generate keys that its hardware couldn’t handle as the root of the issue.

What all that means, in a practical sense, is that anyone could forge an eMudhra certificate to spoof a website and do something malicious. It also means that security researchers who were able to get their hands on devices that still trust eMudhra certificates could have a field day learning how their communications work, which is exactly what Vrátil took advantage of.

eMudhra private keys were added to the open source mitmproxy service - a fully interactive HTTPS proxy that can be used for good or bad - shortly after they were exposed. Pair that with a 2022 Samsung smart TV that still trusts the compromised eMudhra certificates, and you have a way to inspect its HTTPS traffic and redirect selected requests to a server of your choosing.

By Vrátil’s account, swapping out annoying ads for pictures of his family on his TV’s main screen was a pretty simple task.

“Luckily for me, Samsung did not yet release an update for my TV that would revoke the certificate,” Vrátil explained in his writeup. “This allowed me to route all traffic from the TV through mitmproxy and get a list of all the domains and endpoints that my TV talks to, but also see the structure of the requests and response payloads.”

The advertising traffic flow was pretty basic, it turns out: Activity on the TV is relayed to an ad server, which serves up ads on the home screen based on a JSON response. By generating a certificate for Samsung's advertising domains using a compromised eMudhra signing key, and configuring his router to direct requests for those domains to a server on his home network, Vrátil was able to replace ads with family photos served from his NAS. He also added code that tosses other requests to those advertising domains, including tracking data, into a black hole rather than forwarding them to Samsung's servers.

As mentioned above, it’s on GitHub for those who want to trick their TV, if it still supports eMudhra certificates, but you’ll have to do the legwork to dissect how your device is getting ads and tweak the code to work.

“It's not exactly a one-click setup,” Vrátil told The Register in an email. He’s invited people to try it out, but no one has bothered to submit a pull request to add support for their own device to his public repo.

It’s also worth noting that this is only going to work as long as vulnerable devices keep trusting eMudhra certificates, which hopefully means you need to act fast. That said, smart TVs that are out of support may never receive such an update, leaving them exposed to the certificate weakness even if their owners block the ads.

“The compromised eMudhra certificates open up a lot of opportunities for understanding and spoofing network requests from embedded devices, especially those that no longer receive security updates,” Vrátil told us. “And while replacing ads on a TV's home screen with pictures of my family is fun, there are also countless much more sinister applications of this vulnerability.”

As for Vrátil, he’s still trying to figure out how to block the firmware update that may eventually render his method obsolete, even though that, as he points out, is a security risk in and of itself.

“I want to run the traffic through a proxy that would validate the connection against an up-to-date trust store to at least mitigate anyone intercepting traffic from my TV, or spoofing responses, like I do with my little project here, but it won't protect me from other potential security risks, so there's a trade-off,” he explained.

We suppose at this point you can take your pick of abuse. You can use a vulnerability to block ads and some tracking while leaving your TV exposed to potential interception, or let the manufacturer serve up ads and collect data about your viewing habits. There are safer ways to block ads than relying on a TV to keep trusting a compromised CA. ®

articles.title: Halo: Campaign Evolved to Get Firefight as a Free Update
articles.description: When Halo: Campaign Evolved first came out in July it did not include any multiplayer modes, but the first-person shooter remake will at least get Firefight as a free update this Winter.
articles.content:
When Halo: Campaign Evolved first came out in July it did not include any multiplayer modes, but the first-person shooter remake will at least get Firefight as a free update this winter.

Xbox CEO Asha Sharma announced the returning mode in a social media post Thursday, along with a graphic showing a team of Spartans shooting a mix of Covenant and Flood enemies with various guns.

While Firefight isn't the arena competitive multiplayer that most fans had hoped from the Halo remake at launch, wave-based PvE has been a mainstay in the series since Halo 3: ODST in 2009. Essentially, you and your friends load into a map and fight increasingly difficult waves of enemies until you get overwhelmed. There's no reason to believe that this iteration is going to be any different.

Regardless of whether or not Team Deathmatch comes to Halo: Campaign Evolved, this will be the first multiplayer mode to hit the remake, which was pitched primarily as a straight-up revival of the iconic Combat Evolved campaign. Multiplayer was the major piece missing from Campaign Evolved, and this could be a sign that more multiplayer modes will be added in the future.

IGN's Halo: Combat Evolved remake gave it a 7. We said: "Halo: Campaign Evolved speaks to the series' timelessness and adds a decent set of new missions, but it's a mostly a lean retread that's more of a test run for its future with Unreal Engine."

This Firefight announcement comes as Xbox celebrates its 25th anniversary. Earlier today, Sharma looked ahead, predicting "a single person will soon be able to wield capabilities that once required entire nations."

As for Halo, following the summer's drastic cuts at Microsoft's gaming business, Xbox announced a significant reshuffle that saw the next mainline Halo game handed to Call of Duty developer Activision, which is spinning up a new team to work on the franchise. Mass layoffs hit Halo Studios at the same time.

articles.title: New GTA 6 In-Game Footage Continues to Highlight the Game's Unbelievable Graphics
articles.description: Rockstar has released yet another in-game clip from GTA 6, and like yesterday's footage, fans can't quite believe it's real.
articles.content:
Rockstar has released yet another in-game clip from GTA 6, and like yesterday's footage, fans can't quite believe it's real.

This morning, the Instagram account "Only in Dade" (which posts real videos from around Miami, Florida) shared a video of several flashy cars driving around. However, this footage isn't real life; it's actually GTA 6 footage.

The page posted footage of these cars sitting on GTA 6's version of Ocean Drive yesterday while a group of NPCs observed them. Yesterday's footage was actually an in-game recreation of a real video that was posted in October, showing Rockstar's real-life marketing efforts in Miami. Presumably, the new video posted today is also a recreation of a real video from when the real versions of these cars were zooming around the city.

Although the footage doesn't show much, it is an extremely impressive showcase of GTA 6's graphical fidelity. When the first clip dropped yesterday, many thought it was AI or some kind of render. However, it has since been confirmed as authentic gameplay and was reposted by Rockstar itself on Instagram. Fans have reacted to both clips in awe of the visuals, noting that the game has really outdone itself.

"Absolutely insane this is in-game," said one fan in response to the new footage. "This game isn't real, bro; there HAS to be a trap somewhere. There is no f**king way," said another fan in disbelief.

Some have even joked that if this is really how the final game looks, they're more than happy to play it at 30fps. It's clear that Rockstar traded higher performance in favor of visual fidelity, and while that may not be what some fans want, it is inevitably going to result in one of the most graphically advanced games we have ever seen.

Today officially marks exactly one week until GTA 6's release. The game is available to preload right now and it is tracking to have one of the biggest launches in entertainment history. Xbox and PlayStation both confirmed that the game is the most preordered title in the history of their respective stores, and analysts have estimated that the game has already surpassed $1 billion in sales ahead of launch.

Speaking of launch, some game developers are giving their staff the week off to play the game. Palworld developer Pocketpair is one such studio happy to provide extra holiday for the occasion. IGN's latest coverage includes speculation about a potential beloved legacy character from a previous game hiding in the latest GTA 6 trailer.

articles.title: Chainguard defends its choice to break the PHP security embargo: “We own the decision.”
articles.description: At KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026 this week, Chainguard co-founder and CTO Matt Moore defended the company’s decision to The post Chainguard defends its choice to break the PHP security embargo: “We own the decision.” appeared first on The New Stack .
articles.content:
At KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026 this week, Chainguard co-founder and CTO Matt Moore defended the company’s decision to release patched PHP images before an agreed-upon embargo with other partners had lifted.

When Chainguard shipped patched PHP container images more than six hours ahead of an October 21 coordinated security release, PHP’s maintainers accused the company of giving attackers a head start. Chainguard argues attackers already had one.

Chainguard founder and CTO Matt Moore

In an interview with The New Stack, Moore said, “We own the decision that we chose to do it. Nobody could force us to do it — but we did not do it in a vacuum.” He also described, in discussions with TNS, other participants in the embargo and security vendors’ reports of activity targeting the vulnerabilities before Chainguard released its images.

Chainguard was not saying that they patched it faster so they shipped it first. According to Moore, Chainguard believed attackers could already exploit the bugs, or were at least close to figuring out how — or were trying to figure it out.

The two vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 (out-of-memory corruption) and CVE-2026-109619 (stale global state), collectively known as PHP2Shell, were serious memory-management and error-handling flaws. Under the right conditions, an unauthenticated attacker could execute code on a PHP server.

The two bugs involved PHP’s handling of memory exhaustion and its failure to clear references to freed memory between requests. In the first, reaching a memory limit at the wrong moment could interrupt PHP before it finished setting up internal data. Later processing could mistake that unfinished data for valid information. In the second vulnerability, an error could leave PHP holding a reference to memory from an earlier request that had already been freed. A subsequent request could then access that invalid memory. Under exploitable conditions, these failures could let an attacker run code inside the server’s PHP process.

Researchers demonstrated remote code execution through both Apache/mod_php and application-level PHP-FPM paths for the first vulnerability, and against a real-world Apache/mod_php application for the second.

These were problems in PHP itself, not something an administrator could fix by simply updating a WordPress plugin. It was a fundamental and nasty security hole.

How bad were the flaws?

PHP’s advisories rate both vulnerabilities 9.2, or critical, under the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) v4.0. Exploitability depends on the PHP build, server configuration, extensions, and application behavior. The advisories do not establish that every PHP installation can be compromised. PHP released fixes in versions 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27, and 8.5.12. The potential exposure is substantial: As of November 11, W3Techs reported that PHP powered 68.8% of websites whose server-side programming language it could identify.

According to the PHP Foundation’s account, a developer investigating issues from a 2024 security audit spotted the out-of-memory problem, but no concrete attack path was established then. Proposed fixes risked compatibility breaks, new denial-of-service problems, or changes across PHP extensions.

On August 11, Calif researcher Ryan A. reported remote code execution from the same underlying problem. From that date, fixing it became the PHP Foundation security team’s top priority. OpenAI independently reported the same underlying flaw. Wiz supplied additional attack vectors on August 24, and OpenAI reported more on September 18.

How the PHP security patch came apart

In response, PHP’s maintainers coordinated fixes with researchers and distributors. Then details about the release process began leaking.

On October 20, the CVE identifiers circulated publicly, accompanied by an incorrect release time and severity score. PHP responded by issuing a warning and moving the release forward a day, to October 21 at 14:00 UTC. Calif, one of the reporting security companies, then mistakenly published a video demonstrating its proof of concept. Although the video was deleted, copies circulated. PHP also acknowledged that mitigation advice given to critical infrastructure providers might have leaked.

In short, the information environment was already a mess before Chainguard published anything.

But the PHP Foundation maintained that its remaining coordination window still served a purpose: specifically that distributors were packaging the fixes, and releasing immediately would leave many users without a straightforward update path. At 07:41 UTC on October 21, Chainguard published its patched images anyway — six hours and 19 minutes before the agreed-upon time.

The PHP Foundation criticized this move: “Chainguard unilaterally broke the embargo and published built images containing the fix.” That meant, it argued, that “any attacker could now study the fix in binary form while every other PHP user was still waiting for the release.”

A patched binary protects the person who installs it. It can also tell an attacker where to look.

That was the PHP Foundation’s central objection. A patched binary protects the person who installs it. It can also tell an attacker where to look.

Moore’s defense: The advantage had already shifted to the attackers

Moore doesn’t dispute that releasing patched binaries can help attackers. He argues that, by then, the advantage an embargo was supposed to preserve had already eroded.

While defenders alone know about a vulnerability, he told The New Stack, confidentiality gives them time to prepare. Once attackers have enough information to exploit it, withholding available fixes can reverse that advantage: attackers can act, while users outside the embargo cannot protect themselves.

“If we see exploitation in the wild, it’s incumbent upon us to release it,” Moore said. In his account, reports from other security vendors were what pushed Chainguard toward that conclusion.

Moore said Chainguard learned on the Friday before the release that PHP had a vulnerability, pointed its vulnerability-hunting harness at the software, and found the vulnerability or produced a proof of concept within hours. That is Chainguard’s account of its own research. But it helps explain the company’s thinking in breaking the embargo: If your tools can find the bug quickly, you have to consider whether attackers’ tools can too.

He also disputed the implication that Chainguard simply went off on its own. According to Moore, other embargo participants woke Chainguard CEO Dan Lorenc to discuss the situation while PHP maintainers in Europe were asleep. Moore declined to identify those participants.

Moore accepted that Chainguard made the final decision. It does, however, distinguish the company’s account of a disputed emergency decision from an account in which it ignored everyone else without discussion.

The evidence supports concern, not certainty

Public evidence supports Chainguard’s concern that attackers were already targeting the flaws. For example, Amazon Threat Intelligence reported a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt against its MadPot honeypot network on October 17, four days before public disclosure. It also reported proof-of-concept exploits beginning around 02:00 UTC on October 21, followed by additional attempts from anonymized infrastructure over the next six hours. Some of that activity clearly preceded Chainguard’s 07:41 release.

Cloudflare likewise reported observing attack traffic targeting its customers before the official release. It said its free and paid web application firewall protections were enabled by default starting at 03:02 UTC on October 21.

So, no, Chainguard was not imagining hostile interest in these bugs.

But Amazon included an important qualification: “Technical analysis is ongoing, and it’s unclear if any of these attempts would have succeeded in real-world systems.” The PHP security team, meanwhile, said it examined the circulating proofs of concept and “did not identify any functional exploits at the time of release/public disclosure.”

Those statements are not necessarily contradictory. A honeypot can record a request intended to exploit a vulnerability without establishing that it can achieve remote code execution against a real application. Likewise, PHP’s failure to find a functional public exploit does not prove that no attacker privately possessed one.

Subsequent evidence should not be confused with what was known that morning. On October 26, CISA added both vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. That confirms exploitation was known by then; it does not establish when the first successful compromise occurred or whether Chainguard’s early release enabled it.

Welcome to security incident response. The evidence rarely arrives neatly labeled.

Did the binaries give attackers something they lacked?

Moore’s second argument is narrower. Attackers were already probing the relevant code, so publishing patched binaries might not have helped much.

“I don’t see any evidence that what we did helped the attackers in ways that they didn’t already have,” he told TNS. He acknowledged that comparing patched and unpatched binaries can identify vulnerable code, including with AI-assisted disassembly. But identifying the code, he argued, isn’t necessarily the same as building a working exploit.

Fair enough. Locating a memory-corruption bug and reliably turning it into remote code execution are different engineering problems.

Still, this defense has limits. Evidence that some attackers knew where to look does not establish that every prospective attacker did. Nor does it establish that the patch contained no useful clues beyond the vulnerability’s location. Chainguard’s argument depends on how much actionable information was already available and how reliable it was.

The same restraint applies to the accusation against Chainguard. Publishing the binaries created an opportunity to study the changes. It does not, by itself, demonstrate that a particular compromise happened because Chainguard released early.

The two sides were assessing different risks. Chainguard emphasized the danger of withholding a ready patch from users while hostile activity was visible. PHP emphasized the danger of distributing new information before the wider ecosystem could update. Both risks were real.

AI makes the timing problem worse

The broader concern is that AI-assisted vulnerability research could shorten the time defenders have to respond. The public reports cited here do not establish whether the pre-release PHP2Shell attempts used AI, or that this was the first incident of its kind.

For Moore, the PHP dispute fits a larger problem: attackers’ ability to turn vulnerability information into an exploit may outrun defenders’ ability to build and distribute a fix.

He described a scenario in which a Chromium patch becomes public, and an attacker develops an exploit faster than it takes to compile the browser. That was a warning about where the industry is heading, not a claim that this exact scenario had occurred.

“You literally cannot produce builds fast enough,” he said. And the build is only the beginning. Even if Chainguard produces an updated image quickly, customers still have to incorporate it, rebuild their applications, test them, and deploy.

Faster does not mean instantaneous, and a supplier’s release time is not a customer’s remediation time.

That is the uncomfortable part of the “patch faster” answer. Faster is useful. Faster does not mean instantaneous, and a supplier’s release time is not a customer’s remediation time.

Moore’s proposed longer-term response is to reduce the number of vulnerabilities that require this race in the first place. articles.content:
Google’s new Gemini Decisions API, introduced Wednesday, is designed to handle the routine decisions that AI applications make thousands of times a day, with lower costs, and faster response times than traditional generative models.

…the routine decisions that AI applications make thousands of times a day, with lower costs and faster response times than traditional generative models.

Instead of using a generative model to work through each decision and produce a text response, the API uses a new model, Gemini Decision 1, to evaluate predefined options in a single pass.

According to Google, response times range from 150 to 250 milliseconds for tested workloads, while pricing starts at $0.10 per million input tokens with no output-token charges.

The release comes just weeks after OpenAI launched its own Decisions API, joining TypeSafe AI and Microsoft in a growing market for models built to make specific decisions without generating text.

One pass, no generated text

The API supports a 256,000-token context window and can evaluate up to 1,000 independent questions against a single input, including multimodal content. Its responses include probabilities and confidence scores that developers can use to select between predefined options, evaluate information against specific criteria and decide how an application should proceed.

Google CEO Sundar Pichai described the model in a post on X as “built for closed-set choices,” while Google DeepMind product manager Min Choi and principal scientist Felix Yu characterized the API as providing “purpose-built primitives for bounded choices” in the launch announcement.

Where Google already uses it

Google is already using the model internally, including in Gemini Notebook, where real-time model and reasoning-level routing has reportedly reduced latency by up to 40%. Google Search also uses it to detect potentially adversarial behavior involving MCP tools.

Benchmarks come from Google

Google’s benchmark results show Gemini Decision 1 outperforming OpenAI’s GPT-6 Luna, although the competition with TypeSafe’s Jev 1.14 is closer.

Logan Kilpatrick, who leads product for Google AI Studio and the Gemini API, described it on X as “our new frontier decision model in the Gemini API.” On JevBench, Google’s model scored 92.2%, compared with 90.9% for Luna and 90% for Jev.

But Jev came out ahead on two of the seven shared tests and was cheaper to run, costing $0.68 for the full benchmark suite compared with $0.88 for Gemini Decision 1. Google’s model also recorded the lowest calibration error among those tested.

All of the benchmark figures come from Google’s own testing, and independent evaluations have yet to establish how the models compare in production. SiliconANGLE also noted that Jev is cheaper than Google’s model on a per-token basis.

What developers actually pay

Developers only pay to send the shared context once, even when they’re asking multiple questions about it, although the questions themselves still count toward token usage. The API evaluates each question separately, so a workflow that needs to use one answer to decide what to ask next requires another call.

Gemini Decision 1 is available through Google AI Studio, with a free prototyping tier and integrations through OpenRouter, LangChain, Vercel, and LiteLLM. Support for Gemini on Google Cloud is also planned, although Google has not announced a release date.

articles.title: Ebenezer Review
articles.description: Ti West’s Ebenezer does a respectable enough job taking a more horror-forward approach to A Christmas Carol, but the busy Johnny Depp performance at the heart of the film pulls more focus than is necessary.
articles.content:
Ebenezer is in theaters on November 13.

One need only look to The Muppet Christmas Carol, the best Christmas movie of them all, to understand why Charles Dickens’ novella has endured countless adaptations over the nearly two hundred years since it was published. The miserly Ebenezer Scrooge’s confrontation with the ghosts of his past with hopes for a brighter future is so fundamentally strong that a staging of it by Michael Caine and Kermit the Frog that blends all sorts of tones and meta commentary has room not only to work, but to stand as an unambiguously respected adaptation of the text. Ti West’s Ebenezer feels most focused on illuminating the darker corners of Dickens’ tale, but the broad and classically Johnny Depp performance at its heart holds it back from ever elevating into a more meaningful adaptation of the text.

A Christmas Carol is, of course, a ghost story at its heart, and Ti West’s long history in the horror genre - including a ghost story of his own, The Innkeepers - makes him an interesting director to see paired with the material. West’s instincts on how and where to amp up A Christmas Carol’s spooky trappings are strong from the top down, and they’re most evident in Ebenezer’s production design. Ebenezer leans on the austere chill of its Victorian London setting well with practical sets and stages that instantly read as Christmas Carol-appropriate. The destitute and dour look of the film illuminates both the poverty Scrooge hates and the corresponding spiritual bankruptcy from which he suffers in equal measure. Tyler Bates’ string-heavy score helps to push that sense of unease, with the highlight piece being a driving and ominous string quartet version of “Carol of the Bells” played over the opening credits of Londoners bringing out decorations and getting ready for the approaching holiday.

While Ebenezer is largely a faithful adaptation of Dickens’ novella, West and writer Nathaniel Halpern embellish certain turns of the plot to underscore either Scrooge’s inner turmoil or the story’s horror elements, like adding a new prologue featuring Scrooge’s business partner Jacob Marley (Ian McKellen). The prologue serves the dual purpose of starting West’s darker take on the story off with a body (“Marley was dead: to begin with,” and all that) and giving McKellen just a little bit more time on camera. Formative events like Ebenezer’s tough childhood or his failed engagement with Belle get expounded on with enough care to work on their own merits, but with Depp’s Ebenezer tough to connect to emotionally, little of the new additions wind up feeling impactful enough to justify the time spent on them. Despite coming in just under two hours, each of the “staves” that Ebenezer is chaptered into routinely taper off in momentum before West is moving on to the next act of the story.

A director’s influence can only take Ebenezer Scrooge’s story so far. Any staging of A Christmas Carol lives and dies on the casting of its Scrooge: the whole story is told over Scrooge’s shoulder, and whatever catharsis the audience is able to experience through Scrooge’s own as he wakes up on Christmas Day a changed man has to be channeled through an accessible and readably human performance. That leaves Johnny Depp’s work here as Ebenezer Scrooge feeling like a frustrating misfire.

Depp’s conception of Scrooge, with all of its physical business and explosive emotion, feels better suited to stage than screen. Depp’s Scrooge is a constant source of lively and unpredictable energy through the well-trodden events of Ebenezer’s story, it’s just not at all clear by the end of the film that it was the right energy for the more straightforward approach West employs throughout the rest of the film. Depp’s conception of Scrooge, with all of its physical business and explosive emotion, feels better suited to stage than screen. What’s all the more frustrating is that Depp is not only capable of stepping down the zaniness of his Scrooge when called on, but he’s far better in the role when doing so. The few moments throughout the film where Depp plays Scrooge with some reserve, like when trying to break through to his past selves to beg them to do things differently, connect pretty effectively, and the final stretch where Scrooge is able to rejoice in his overnight rebirth gives Depp’s manic approach to the character a better fitting context.

With Depp’s campy performance pushing Ebenezer’s otherwise macabre presentation to its breaking point, supporting players like Rupert Grint, Ellie Bamber, and Sam Claflin do a lot to keep the story grounded in more recognizable feelings. Grint’s affability as Scrooge’s clerk Bob Cratchit cuts Depp’s hissing negativity well, and Ebenezer could have used more of the genuine light that he and the Cracthit family contributes, if only for the contrast to make all of the film’s darkness feel that much more oppressive.

On that note, points to whoever was responsible for casting Freddie Lee-Grey as Tiny Tim: he has nary more to say than “god bless us, everyone”, but wow, does that kid step up to the plate and knock it out of the park when called to do so. As Scrooge’s nephew Fred, Claflin embodies the optimism and good nature that Scrooge detests with ease, with Daisy Ridley stopping by for what amounts to a cameo as Fred’s more skeptical wife Clara and walking away with one of the film’s bigger laughs. Bamber’s Belle is just as effective as Fred at portraying the warmth that Scrooge willingly and cruelly let go of years before.

West makes no attempt to give the spirits that visit Ebenezer any cheery or pleasant characteristics: they’re dead and they hate it, and from the looks of them, they have good reason to feel that way. McKellen’s Marley does get a brief moment to act as a canary in a moral coalmine for Scrooge early on, but he’s mostly here to lend some gravitas to the obligatory “you will be haunted by three spirits” moment, the kind of thing he’s been doing in his sleep for decades. Not helping his efforts at all are the cheap-looking visual effects doing the work to create McKellen’s spectral form. The poor quality of the visual effects extends to the dozens of nameless ghosts that arrive to put the fear of Father Christmas in Scrooge’s heart by banging on windows and going “ooh” and “ahh”, plaguing both he and the audience throughout the film.

Thankfully, the headliner Ghosts of Christmases Past, Present, and Yet to Come are better designed and realized. Andrea Riseborough’s bride-like Ghost of Christmas Past is the most outwardly eerie, with milky eyes and a detached, childlike voice which really cut through Depp’s bombast as Scrooge revisits a painful chapter of his younger days. Riseborough’s performance is monotone by design, but West supports Risebrough’s ethereal presence with some of the film’s more outwardly horror-coded cinematography, with some effective long takes that pull a sort of “Texas switch” by having her teleport quickly and creepily across long distances. Tramell Tillman’s Ghost of Christmas Present is more mercurial, and Tillman’s intensity and lack of patience with Scrooge’s waffling both give the sense that he could throttle Scrooge at the drop of a nightcap. The Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come maintains the slow-moving, wordless and faceless presentation it usually does, but West at least gives it a haunting Predator-like clicking sound to set it apart.

articles.description: Disney has announced its plans for the 50th anniversary of Star Wars, which will include a fresh documentary detailing the making of A New Hope.
articles.content:
Disney has announced its plans for the 50th anniversary of Star Wars, which will include a fresh documentary detailing the making of A New Hope.

George Lucas' original Star Wars film debuted back in 1977, kicking off what would become one of the world's most popular and lucrative film and TV franchises. Half a century on, Disney+ will debut "The Hero Awakens," a brand-new documentary featuring rare archival footage from A New Hope's production, helmed by Academy Award-nominated filmmaker R.J. Cutler.

The Hero Awakens will drop via Disney+ on Star Wars' annual May 4th celebration, following the theatrical re-release of Star Wars on February 19. This will be the rarely-seen original 1977 version of the movie — back when Jabba the Hutt was not a CGI slug and Greedo actually shot first.

In terms of what's actually new for the Star Wars franchise next year, Ahsoka Season 2 will drop via Disney+ on January 20, while Star Wars: Starfighter will land in theaters on May 28.

Both are anticipated, though will arrive at a time of great uncertainty for the Star Wars franchise in general, following the decidedly mixed response to Disney's sequel trilogy, several short-lived Disney+ TV projects, and a lengthy slate of movie projects cancelled or stuck in development hell. Not even a big screen outing for The Mandalorian and Grogu this year could turn things around, as the movie set a rather disappointing record for the franchise's lowest live-action theatrical gross.

Looking further ahead, a press release for Star Wars' 50th anniversary states that 2027 will bring a year of "new project announcements, anniversary merchandise, dedicated fan events, archival releases, and reimagined Disney Parks and Cruiseline offerings." Exactly what these project announcements are remains to be seen, though it seems likely we'll get a sense of the franchise's future before next year is out.

With Ahsoka and Starfighter the only remaining live-action Star Wars TV and movie projects publicly announced, the time has certainly come for Lucasfilm's newly-installed co-president Dave Filoni to map out what's next. Reports suggest that of everything Lucasfilm has previously announced, the new movie/trilogy written by Dark Phoenix's Simon Kinberg is the one currently moving forward.

articles.title: Microsoft has an image problem with November's Windows security update
articles.description: Zero-size graphics can derail printing, while some admins also face activation failures
articles.content:
Printing with Windows has always been something of a choose-your-own-adventure, and November's security update has added another unwelcome plot twist: documents containing certain images might not print.

The issue affects images rendered with a height or width of zero at the selected printing resolution. These might not be visible to users, but can form part of a document's watermarking or layout.

After the update, those invisible objects can apparently make the printed document disappear too. Microsoft said: "The issue was observed when printing Microsoft Word documents using the Windows Graphics Device Interface (GDI), but printing from other applications might also be affected."

According to the notification (WI1549472), most versions of Windows are affected, from the latest Windows 11 26H2 through Windows 10 Enterprise LTSC 2016. Windows Server from 2025 to 2016 is also affected.

Users need not have added these objects themselves. Microsoft says document-generation tools can insert them even when no graphic is visible.

Printer problems aren't the only issue requiring attention. After installation of the November 2026 security update, Microsoft warned that "certain Windows activation and licensing operations performed using the Software Licensing Management Tool (SLMGR) might fail."

This one is a little more niche, but it could be a headache for affected administrators. It primarily affects organizations that use command-line tools or automated processes to manage Windows activation and licensing.

"Affected devices might encounter error 0x80041008, Invalid parameter ( SWbemObjectEx ), when running commands to activate Windows, configure Key Management Service (KMS), or manage product keys," Microsoft said. "The failure has been observed while executing the command ' slmgr.vbs /skms-domain ' and ' slmgr.vbs /ipk '."

The notice (WI1549486) currently lists Windows 11 23H2, Windows 10 22H2 and 21H2, and Windows Server 2025, 2022, and 2019 as affected.

The printing problem remains under investigation, but Microsoft says a fix for the activation issue is due in the coming days. Administrators needing an interim workaround must contact Microsoft Support for Business. ®

articles.description: Today, we’re talking about the Jensen Huang scandal at Nvidia, which is developing so quickly that we had to do an emergency update of this intro minutes before publishing this episode. Huang just resigned from his position as CEO of Nvidia as news of his affairs, including with an alleged Chinese s
articles.content:
Today, we’re talking about the Jensen Huang scandal at Nvidia, which is developing so quickly that we had to do an emergency update of this intro minutes before publishing this episode.

Huang just resigned from his position as CEO of Nvidia as news of his affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy, threatened to engulf the company.

We’ll have more on that story as things develop and we learn how Nvidia will restructure itself after Jensen — he had something like 60 direct reports, after all, and the entire AI financial ecosystem flows through the company. This is pure Decoder bait.

But just two days ago I talked to Kyle Chan, a foreign policy fellow at the Brookings Institution’s John L. Thornton China Center, about the real heart of the scandal: What would China even seek to accomplish by having a spy so close to Jensen? And what does the real state of the US-China AI conflict really looks like, particularly from the Chinese point of view?

Kyle’s answers about chips and how China is perceiving the so-called AI “race” were very illuminating, but maybe even more interesting was his observation on Jensen Huang’s relationship with Trump was the most important thing of all — because maybe what China most stood to gain was someone who could whisper in the right ears.

Let’s just dive right into it. But keep in mind that when we were talking, we still didn’t know what would happen with Jensen.

Okay: Kyle Chan on Nvidia, China, and the future of AI export controls. Here we go.

This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Kyle Chan, you are a fellow at the John L. Thornton China Center at the Brookings Institution. Welcome to Decoder.

Great to be here.

What on earth could we be talking about as it relates to your expertise about China today? I have a lot to ask you about Nvidia, about our relationship to China as a country, as an economy, and about national security.

Let’s start at the very beginning. From all the reporting we have today, it seems like the United States government has been very worried about a company called Megaspeed and Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese spy at the center of the swirling scandal around Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia. What do we know about Alice Huang and Megaspeed?

We have to be careful about what we know and what we don’t know. So far, there are allegations that the US intelligence community believes that Alice Huang may be an asset of the Chinese intelligence services. Megaspeed itself is a customer of Nvidia’s and they built a data center in Malaysia.

They also seem to potentially have ties with Chinese companies and could — and this is where we’re getting into what we do know and what we don’t know — potentially be a conduit for Chinese AI companies accessing cutting-edge Nvidia chips like Blackwells.

Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free  Decoder  wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.

I want to rewind way back. The notion that the Chinese AI industry wants Nvidia chips has been floating around for years and the idea that the Chinese AI industry would somehow develop a parallel set of technology or a superior set of technology because of the constraint of not having Nvidia chips has percolated into the discourse several times.

I’m particularly thinking about DeepSeek. DeepSeek launched R1 and it outperformed our models in some ways. We think they didn’t have access to the chips. There are some accusations that they had access to the chips. It turns out they did a bunch of fine-tuning on the chips they did have.

What is that relationship like? Do they need the highest-end Nvidia chips? Is it true that they’re actually developing parallel technologies that might be superior to the chips they can have? Just set that stage.

A lot of the details are murky, and they’re probably murky for a reason. But up until now, we saw Chinese AI companies that were very heavily dependent on Nvidia chips in order to train and run their models. In fact, they became some of the biggest contributors to the CUDA ecosystem, which is Nvidia’s software ecosystem and platform.

They got very good at that, but at the same time with US export controls and greater technology restrictions on access to cutting-edge GPUs, China increasingly pushed these AI companies to switch away from Nvidia to Huawei and other domestic AI chip makers. The idea there is to develop a parallel domestic AI chip supply chain that is good enough, if not on par with, Nvidia’s latest chips, and — crucially — resilient to policy actions coming out of Washington.

So that is the story up until this point. The question is, now, what is that trajectory for the Chinese GPU or AI chip development?

The reason I wanted to start there is that the motivations to get close to Jensen Huang are very murky to me. As the CEO of Nvidia, I understand that everyone thinks he’s the character and he’s actually in the software designing the next generation of Nvidia GPUs, but he’s just traveling the world giving policy speeches.

If you want to build a parallel GPU ecosystem, you’re trying to get close to the designers and the engineers, right? What would be the goal of trying to get close to Jensen Huang?

If you wanted the design specs for the latest Nvidia GPUs, I don’t know if you would ask Jensen directly. I think you might want to go to his technical staff.

He does have like 60 direct reports. Decoder is often a show about org charts and that one has been on top of my list for a long time, but we’ll set that aside for now. Keep going.

What it’s really about is potentially two things. One is trying to understand, maybe to glean information about, the US policymaking process. Jensen Huang is very close to Trump. They talk a lot. Trump can apparently just call Jensen on his cell phone at any moment.

In the middle of a conference. We’ve seen the video.

On the other side, and maybe this is even the bigger issue, perhaps it’s the biggest concern of all, is the concern that the direction of movement could run the other way, which is that somehow through Jensen, China might be able to influence US policymaking, especially on export controls. That is the big worry from a lot of people in Washington.

One of the other underlying concerns here, that I’m just trying to parse out, is that Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese spy, is an executive at a company called Megaspeed. And through Megaspeed, Nvidia may have already been circumventing export controls.

It seems like if you’re already solving the problem, maybe you should just leave it alone. How does that dynamic play out?

A lot of the story is strange. Even seen in the most cynical terms, it doesn’t quite add up. There could be several different possibilities. One is that this is actually not some concerted strategy from Beijing to try to obtain chips or information or influence, but this is potentially Beijing not quite understanding the full situation and wanting to co-op this Alice Huang person and at least try to understand from her standpoint what is happening.

Because I think you’re right. Already you have a very strong relationship between Nvidia and Megaspeed. You also already have — and this is on the influence side — Jensen Huang advocating for his own commercial interests, for a loosening of export controls on his own chips to China. You don’t really need Beijing to push on that gas pedal. That’s already happening.

So there are some things that don’t quite make sense if you’re thinking about it from those standpoints, but if you’re thinking about it from the viewpoint of “Beijing wants visibility,” then perhaps that is another plausible explanation.

Beijing just wants someone who Trump calls on the phone to advocate for their viewpoints. I see all of that, but what are we getting out of it? If the goal is Nvidia chips, it feels like that is already assured. If the goal is Nvidia engineering plans, that feels like a question mark. If the goal is influence over the Trump administration, I feel like they could have just bought cryptocurrency.

[Laughs] That’s right.

There’s a big swirl of what is actually happening here. Maybe your point that Beijing just needed more visibility because it is a swirl is the motivating factor. The question that leads me to is that the New York Times reports that US intelligence agencies first flagged these issues a year ago to the Trump administration. There was a memo from Marco Rubio. The reporting is that he oversaw the memo, which is as much plausible deniability as anything. He oversaw it. He was aware that there was a memo. A year ago, the United States’ national security apparatus was worried about Alice Huang at Megaspeed, her relationship with Jensen, and nothing occurred. What do you make of that?

That is one of the most worrying aspects of all this. Regardless of what the details are and what is known publicly versus what our intelligence community knows, this is something that should be investigated. This is obviously a major national security issue and this is something where you don’t want someone meddling with this process. You want to do a full investigation, get to the bottom of what’s happening.

I think what we’re seeing from some of the reporting is that this has been known, and in fact, if anything, there may have been efforts to try to stop this investigation or distort it in some way. That is very troubling from that internal, within-the-US-government perspective.

There’s a lot going on with Nvidia in that part of the story, where Nvidia’s own spokespeople are saying, “There’s nothing going on here. This is a normal relationship,” on the record to many publications. A week later, Jensen issues his apology letter saying there was a relationship.

That’s not great for John Rizzo, Nvidia’s comms person. Tim Teter, Nvidia’s general counsel, is out there saying everything is above board. Now we know not everything is above board. What do you make of Nvidia’s corporate governance here? Because there’s a whole bunch of shareholder lawsuits to come. There’s one filed as of today. I can only imagine there are more to come.

Nvidia has to tread very carefully here because what you don’t want is exactly what’s already happening, which is to start to deny or dismiss some of these issues and then turn around and have to say, “Actually, there might be something there.”

This is especially important now as there are growing calls for a congressional investigation. So this is going to be separate, perhaps, from within the executive branch where, again, I think we have reasons to worry about conflicts of interest and people not wanting to do this all the way. But if there’s a full-blown congressional investigation, that might reveal some things that, if you are Nvidia, you want to get out in front of rather than have to backpedal later on and explain yourself.

Part of the back and forth here with the government’s concern about Alice Huang and Megaspeed is that the Commerce Department spent months looking at the company and then Teter, the general counsel of Nvidia, emailed them and invoked a direct relationship with the Commerce undersecretary, Jeff Kessler. That got the case kicked to the DOJ where everything stopped.

Trump yesterday said the FBI is investigating — that’s obviously connected to the DOJ. There’s a universe where the Trump administration is trying to make this go away. Nvidia can pressure the Trump administration to make this go away. That reeks of corruption, obviously.

And then you have a very empowered class of Democrats coming into Congress with polling that suggested corruption was one of the top issues in this last election. I don’t see any outcome except those Democrats and an empowered bunch of investigators and an empowered bunch of committee chairs coming after Nvidia as hard as they can.

articles.title: President Trump says Apple’s Tim Cook is the only man to replace Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO
articles.description: President Trump says Tim Cook should replace Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia.
articles.content:
President Donald Trump has said that retired Apple CEO Tim Cook should replace Jensen Huang as the CEO of Nvidia, just hours after it was announced that the latter had resigned in the wake of a series of scandals. Taking to his Truth Social platform, the President said, "NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place - TIM COOK of Apple. A Legend replaces a Legend! President DONALD J. TRUMP."

Nvidia's board of directors announced on Wednesday that Huang had resigned following the revelation that he conducted an extramarital affair with a Megaspeed executive suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset, and a further affair with Nvidia Vice President of Health Care, Kimberly Powell.

Colette Kress, Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer, will serve as Interim CEO while the company looks for a replacement. Naturally, names have been floated as potential successor candidates, including Apple's Chief Hardware Officer Johny Srouji.

With Nvidia at the center of the global explosion in AI, Huang and Trump have enjoyed a close relationship that routinely makes news headlines. Trump previously described Huang as 'utterly visionary' in regard to his views on tariffs and rescinding President Biden's AI Diffusion Rule.

President Trump's name has been mentioned in the ongoing Huang affair scandal. Notably, it is alleged that while U.S. intelligence believed that Huang had been the target of a Chinese honeypot operation, reports claim that President Trump was briefed on the matter but chose not to do anything with the information, so as not to affect Nvidia's sales or antagonize China.

Congress has summoned Jensen Huang to appear before the Select Committee on the CCP, with lawmakers threatening to issue Huang with a subpoena if he doesn't agree to attend a closed-door meeting voluntarily.

Tim Cook is currently the Executive Chair of Apple's board, having served as the company's CEO from 2011 to 2026. During his tenure, he oversaw the launch of a plethora of Apple services, including Apple Music and Apple TV, while expanding into new product categories such as Apple Watch and AirPods.

Nvidia's share price plunged more than 10 percentage points at the open on Wednesday, but recovered much of that ground as traders looked to take advantage of the dip in Nvidia's share price. The company will report its third-quarter fiscal 2027 financial results next week, on Tuesday, November 17.

articles.title: Elon Musk says it ‘would be an honor’ to hire ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang
articles.description: A random X poster urged Elon Musk to hire Jensen Huang just hours before the former Nvidia chief resigned from his position.
articles.content:
Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO two weeks after his relationship with a suspected Chinese spy was revealed by intelligence sources and a day after his affair with an Nvidia vice president became publicly known. But hours before this move, when it was just rumored that the Nvidia board was planning to oust him, Elon Musk had already stated his willingness to hire the former Nvidia chief on X. A random X user posted, “Elon please hire Jensen,” to which the billionaire replied, “That would be an honor.”

@zerohedge That would be an honor November 12, 2026

Despite the scandals that Jensen is currently facing, he still has the engineering know-how, deep knowledge of the industry and its inner workings, plus multiple connections across the world, which would be extremely valuable for any company looking to break into the semiconductor industry.

This is exactly what Elon Musk is doing with his Terafab project, which he first mentioned in November 2025. Jensen Huang even warned that this was going to be a challenge, pointing out that “the engineering, the science, and the artistry of doing what TSMC does for a living is extremely hard.” Nevertheless, Musk poured his resources into the project, with construction on the Terafab facility in full swing and with plans to hit volume chip production by the second half of 2028. Musk himself said that the site targets a production capacity of a million wafers a month by 2032. Tesla has an ambitious AI accelerator roadmap, and SpaceX has even touted making its own GPUs in the future.

We still don’t know what Jensen Huang’s plans are, but even though he’s no longer a part of the Nvidia board and its leadership, Jensen and his wife, Lori, still jointly own approximately 800 million Nvidia shares through various trusts and LLCs, while Huang himself personally owns around 70 million Nvidia shares.

Aside from that, he still has an outstanding invitation from Congress to discuss Nvidia’s security protocols, which could turn into a subpoena if he snubs them, although we don’t know how his resignation would affect the closed-door meeting. There’s also a reported FBI investigation into his relationship with Alice Huang, the Megaspeed executive who was allegedly instrumental in the import of $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia AI GPUs into China and is suspected of working with China’s Ministry of State Security.

Jensen Huang is just the latest in the long list of executives who resigned or were ousted from their leadership position because of a relationship or an affair with a subordinate. This includes former Boeing CEO Harry Stonecipher in 2005, HP CEO Mark Hurd in 2010, Intel CEO Brian Krzanich in 2018, and former McDonald’s CEO Steve Easterbrook in 2019. Musk himself is known to have had relationships with subordinates from his various companies, and that he has even fathered four children with Shivon Zilis, a top executive at Neuralink who started working at Tesla in 2017, through IVF.

It’s still not confirmed if Musk’s reply is a serious offer for Jensen Huang. But if the former Nvidia chief ever decides to work for Musk on his Terafab project, then Jensen could put his effort and expertise into turning it into a formidable competitor to Nvidia.

articles.title: United Airlines wants you to check in, not your chatbot
articles.description: AI agents face restrictions over safety checks that require a human touch
articles.content:
United Airlines has become the latest company to slap restrictions on unauthorized third-party AI agents, warning that the bots could make unintended purchases, expose customer data, or bypass checks requiring human acknowledgment.

The airline announced restrictions covering both its own digital platforms and indirect access through travel agencies and aggregators, with changes to its booking, ticketing, and distribution policies.

United says automated actions could violate aviation regulations, citing the requirement for a human acknowledgment during check-in that bags contain no banned substances. A bot cheerfully ticking the box isn't quite the passenger confirmation it has in mind.

And then there is the worry that "sharing account credentials with personal, third-party, AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles."

United would also rather customers use its own app than turn third-party assistants loose on its systems.

AI agents are pitched as a way to outsource life's minutiae, and it's difficult to navigate the web without tripping over a breathless influencer explaining why you need one, or dozens, or hundreds of virtual personal assistants.

The thing is that operating these assistants requires care and thought. Earlier this year, British mathematician Professor Hannah Fry conducted a cautionary experiment in which she gave an AI agent a bank card, and a bit too much agency, to see what it would do. Passwords were coughed up, and some ill-considered purchases were made. Still, as Fry said of the agent, dubbed Cassandra, "don't let her incompetence fool you, because these things are getting better fast."

Last month, reports emerged of major US banks blocking third-party AI agents from operating inside accounts and taking actions on behalf of the customer. This month, several UK banks were reported to have followed suit.

United stated: "Corporate leaders in the banking and retail industries have taken similar actions regarding AI agents and we encourage others to consider measures that preserve the data and security of their customers and strengthen safety."

The Register asked United Airlines how it planned to implement the blocking. There are a few options, including physical biometric confirmation for actions or checking for signs of automated browser driving. Amazon has also moved against unauthorized AI agents, blocking Meta's Muse (the "AI that gets it done," according to Meta's marketing) in September.

The airline has yet to respond. ®
