articles.title: The death of the 14-day patch: Surviving machine-speed vulnerability discovery
articles.description: For decades, enterprise vulnerability management ran on human time: A security researcher manually dissected a binary, traced execution paths, built The post The death of the 14-day patch: Surviving machine-speed vulnerability discovery appeared first on The New Stack .
articles.content:
For decades, enterprise vulnerability management ran on human time: A security researcher manually dissected a binary, traced execution paths, built a proof of concept, and filed a coordinated disclosure. Engineering leads evaluated the CVSS score and prioritized the fi before working it into an upcoming sprint schedule. Then, finally, they shipped the update.

That deliberate cadence is a thing of the past.

In the first nine months of 2026, publishers recorded 75,242 CVEs, representing roughly 20% of all vulnerabilities published since the CVE program was established in 1999.

The acceleration is steepening: according to the Cyber Strategy Institute, nearly 38,000 of those flaws surfaced in Q3 alone.

“The pace of vulnerability discovery has outpaced the human capacity to remediate it. Engineering organizations face a stark operational reality: the traditional two-week patch cycle is dead.”

The pace of vulnerability discovery has outpaced the human capacity to remediate it. Engineering organizations face a stark operational reality: the traditional two-week patch cycle is dead.

Why vulnerabilities exploded in 2026

This surge is not caused by developers writing worse code. It is the direct result of vulnerability hunting transforming from an artisan craft into an autonomous, distributed compute problem.

Autonomous codebase traversal: Legacy SAST tools flooded dashboards with noisy pattern matches. Modern agentic security systems run full-context semantic analysis: cloning repositories, tracing asynchronous data flows across microservices, constructing dynamic exploit payloads in sandboxes, and confirming exploitability before ever raising an alert.

Exhaustive compute at scale: Compute does not tire. Swarms of automated agents continuously traverse open-source package registries and public repositories, decompiling transitive dependencies, auditing legacy C/C++ utilities, and testing modern Go, Rust, and Node.js runtimes for concurrency bugs, deserialization flaws, and memory leaks.

Focus on foundational infrastructure: Autonomous discovery focuses heavily on high-leverage software targets, identity layers, reverse proxies, parsers, and container runtimes.

“This surge is not caused by developers writing worse code. It is the direct result of vulnerability hunting transforming from an artisan craft into an autonomous, distributed compute problem.”

When machines search exhaustively across the entire public software graph, they will discover every reachable flaw.

The operational cascade

The deluge of machine-discovered CVEs creates severe structural friction across risk management, engineering velocity, and compliance:

The exposure gap becomes unmanageable: As detailed in analysis on the expanding CVE exposure gap, the critical hazard is the elapsed time between public exploit discovery and downstream production deployment. When agentic frameworks generate working zero-day or N-day exploits within hours of a code push, a multi-day patching window is an open door.

Alert paralysis and triage debt: Engineering teams are trapped between CVSS scores (which measure theoretical severity) and EPSS metrics (which predict real-world exploitation likelihood). Discerning whether an alert represents an unreachable helper function or an active, weaponizable zero-click flaw has turned routine triage into continuous crisis management.

Compliance and audit deadlock: Frameworks like NIST SP 800-53 (Control SI-2), PCI-DSS 4.0, and DORA enforce strict timelines for critical and high-severity issues. When 9.0+ CVSS scores arrive in weekly batches, security and platform leads spend more time writing risk-acceptance waivers than hardening production architecture.

Can internal IT teams keep up with patching and push innovation?

The short answer is no.

Enterprise development exists to deliver business value: ship differentiated features, enhance platform reliability, and expand market share.

Yet today’s software supply chains rely on thousands of dependencies. When a critical flaw lands in foundational infrastructure, such as an authentication engine, an API gateway, or a database driver, feature roadmaps freeze. Development teams are forced into fire drills:

Halt active sprint work.

Trace internal dependencies to determine real exploitability.

Reconcile dependency breaks, merge conflicts, and integration regressions.

Execute emergency deployments across multi-region production clusters.

Defending against automated, machine-speed discovery using manual human labor is an economic dead end.

The architectural shift: Decoupling architecture from maintenance

Open-source software (OSS) remains a foundation of enterprise computing, but self-hosting foundational components introduces an unsustainable operational tax: you become the de facto maintainer of every layer you host.

To withstand the automated vulnerability era, forward-looking engineering teams are changing their operating model: preserve open standards and architectures, but outsource the patching burden.

1. Managed platform tiers for critical edge and identity

Foundational edge components, such as identity and authorization planes (e.g., Ory Kratos/Hydra) or ingress proxies (e.g., Envoy), form an organization’s perimeter. When implementation flaws or protocol vulnerabilities hit these layers, maintaining self-hosted community forks requires constant emergency rebuilds. Shifting these layers to managed vendor clouds offloads zero-day mitigation, regression testing, and upstream backporting to teams dedicated entirely to that software layer.

2. Commercial subscriptions with contractual backporting SLAs

For organizations restricted by strict data sovereignty, air-gapped data centers, or zero-trust VPC policies, public SaaS is not always an option. However, relying purely on raw community repositories leaves internal teams subject to unpredictable release cycles and breaking updates.

A viable hybrid approach is adopting commercial open-source enterprise subscriptions backed by formal CVE remediation SLAs (such as Red Hat Enterprise Linux, enterprise distributions of Kubernetes, or commercial licenses like the Ory Enterprise License ). Organizations retain full control over their data plane while outsourcing patch engineering:

Predictable remediation SLAs: Contractual response windows for High and Critical vulnerabilities replace upstream community best-effort timelines.

Non-breaking LTS backports: Vendors backport security fixes directly to long-term support branches, eliminating the breaking schema changes and API refactors that accompany major upstream updates.

Verified distribution streams: Access to signed SBOMs and hardened enterprise container images reduces internal triage friction in CI/CD pipelines.

3. Continuous delivery automation and runtime shielding

For internally maintained services, teams must automate the path from patch to production. This requires pairing automated GitOps workflows (e.g., ArgoCD, Renovate) with progressive deployment controllers (like Flagger or Argo Rollouts) and eBPF-based runtime shielding (such as Cilium Tetragon). Automated canary verification and kernel-level network enforcement isolate vulnerabilities in flight, buying engineers time to test and deploy updates without emergency rollouts.

Fighting automation with automation

The volume of vulnerability disclosures will not return to human scale. As autonomous models and agentic fuzzing advance, exploit discovery and weaponization will move faster still.

“The volume of vulnerability disclosures will not return to human scale. The sustainable path forward requires matching automation with automation: modernize the stack so upstream infrastructure partners absorb the patching burden.”

Attempting to absorb this flood with manual Jira tickets and emergency weekend deployments guarantees developer burnout and security breaches. The sustainable path forward requires matching automation with automation: modernize the stack so upstream infrastructure partners absorb the patching burden, allowing internal engineering teams to focus on what matters… shipping product.

articles.title: Microsoft Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 enter their 'permanently vulnerable' era
articles.description: Upgrade, migrate, but don't prevaricate – time has run out
articles.content:
Microsoft has warned customers still clinging to Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 to consider the software "permanently vulnerable" as November's security fixes arrive for Subscription Edition (SE) alone.

The warning appears in the release documentation for November's Exchange Server SE security update.

Looking for Exchange 2016 and 2019 information? Tough. Microsoft stated: "Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 are no longer tested for vulnerabilities and there are no updates released. If you are using those versions of Exchange, you should consider them permanently vulnerable [Microsoft's emphasis] and should upgrade your organization immediately." You have been warned.

Support for Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 ended on October 14, 2025, but the company announced an Extended Security Updates (ESU) program in July 2025. The plan was that this program would end on April 14, 2026, by which time customers would surely have made the jump to a later or online version, right? The company said: "This period will not be extended past April 2026 (you do not need to ask)."

And... of course it was. As April 2026 rolled around, and it became clear that some customers were still stubbornly sticking with the old versions, Microsoft did the equivalent of heaving an exasperated sigh and offered another six months of paid security updates. Those final weeks also brought a separate treat: a Windows Server update breaking Exchange Server.

This time it was serious. Microsoft released the final Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 security updates on October 13. No more patches, no more vulnerability testing, and apparently no more reprieves.

According to Microsoft's Security Update Guide, the November update fixed nine vulnerabilities in Exchange Server SE, including a critical remote code execution flaw, CVE-2026-118207. Microsoft isn't testing earlier versions of Exchange for the vulnerabilities. ®

articles.title: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia chief executive
articles.description: 'Next week’s earnings call just became the most important in the company’s history'
articles.content:
Nvidia's Jensen Huang has resigned as CEO of the company, following the revelation of his affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy and reports of a relationship with another woman who was a company employee.

In a Form 8-K [PDF] filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), the GPU maker disclosed that it accepted the resignation of Huang, whom it identified as Jen-Hsun Huang, on November 11, effective immediately.

He is being replaced by chief financial officer Colette Kress, who will serve as interim leader while the board conducts a search for a new CEO.

Huang, who founded Nvidia in 1993 and served as president, CEO, and a member of the board of directors ever since, led the GPU maker to become one of the most valuable companies in the world, hitting a hit peak of over $5.5 trillion earlier this year.

His position became untenable following an investigation by the company's board after he admitted to an affair, amid allegations he had a romantic relationship with a woman the US authorities suspected as a Chinese spy.

Reports later surfaced this week of a second alleged affair with an employee of the company itself, reported by the New York Times as being with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care.

A two-week downfall

News of the scandal first broke barely a couple of weeks ago, on October 29, when claims surfaced that Huang had been the target of an espionage plot involving a Chinese businesswoman working for a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed which was a customer of Nvidia.

According to the New York Times, US intelligence had reason to believe the woman, Alice Huang, was recruited to gather information about Nvidia and its operations for the Beijing government. Megaspeed also faces claims it was illicitly shipping Nvidia products to China, in violation of US export controls.

Any relationship between Huang and a Chinese operative would be enormously concerning, as the US has been trying to keep advanced technology for AI out of the hands of the country, allegedly for security reasons, fearing it might be used for military purposes.

For its part, Beijing rejects the spying allegations, saying they are part of a smear campaign against China.

Shortly after Nvidia’s board announced it was investigating Huang, he sent an email to Nvidia staff apologizing and confessing to having an affair, though he did not explicitly name Alice Huang in his public apology.

It seemed like the leather-jacketed leader might just hang on, since it was difficult to imagine anyone other than him leading the company after all this time. But Nvidia’s shares fell 4.3 percent on November 9 and a further 5.5 percent the following day, wiping around $430 billion off its market value, amid all the speculation.

Then the claim emerged regarding a second affair, with an employee at Nvidia who reported to him, and many commentators took it as a sign the game was up. Huang resigned the same day the news broke.

Indecision ahead

Now the speculation starts over who will take over the reins at Nvidia, but Huang could prove a tough act to follow. He is said to have recognized early on the potential for taking the number-crunching capabilities of graphics processors and putting them to use at accelerating AI processing, and Nvidia’s position today as the leading AI hardware firm is thanks to that bet.

“The sudden resignation of Jensen Huang is about more than succession at the world’s most important AI chipmaker, Nvidia’s leadership crisis is a stress test for the AI boom,” says Forrester VP and group research director Stephanie Balaouras.

If Nvidia stabilizes quickly under new leadership, the AI infrastructure boom will have demonstrated resilience, she adds. But if its stock or financing relationships remain under sustained pressure, that would add evidence to the fragility of the AI bubble.

“In the near term, the board did the sensible thing and reached for a steward. Colette Kress knows every number in that order book,” commented Mark Malek, CIO at financial services firm Siebert Financial.

“It does NOT settle the stock. Interim means the real decision is still ahead, the investigations are still open, and next week’s earnings call just became the most important in the company’s history,” he added. ®

They take the stage at 10 a.m. Pacific on Tuesday, November 17.

After the opening keynote, you can experience how customers put AI into production at scale, see where Microsoft is taking the tools those customers use, and compare notes with industry colleagues already doing the work. The breakout sessions (and hallway networking) offer the opportunity to double-click into results after an actual deployment.

With the rapid advancement of AI tools and resources, the best playbook is often the one your peers have already tested. Microsoft Ignite gives leaders a place to compare deployment strategies and lessons learned face to face, with organizations just getting started and others already getting results from AI in production.

Microsoft tells The New Stack that over four days, more than 100 organizations will take the stage across keynotes, breakout sessions and theater stages.

Microsoft tells The New Stack that over four days, more than 100 organizations will take the stage across keynotes, breakout sessions and theater stages. The organizations span AI startups such as Replit and Harvey, financial firms including Morgan Stanley and BNY, and companies such as Toyota and Siemens. If you’re choosing a first project (or deciding which pilot deserves more budget), the range at Ignite should give you a chance to gauge how teams with different goals are making those same decisions you’re facing.

How Microsoft AI solutions work together

Microsoft calls its approach Frontier Transformation. It starts with what people want to accomplish, the information AI agents need to help them, and finally, the controls an organization needs once AI is in use.

For employees, Microsoft 365 Copilot puts AI into tools they already use, including Teams and Word. Microsoft Fabric brings business data and analytics together, and Microsoft IQ gives Copilot and agents context, pulling from in-house data, workplace activity, documents, and the web. Developers can use GitHub and GitHub Copilot to write and review code, then use Microsoft Foundry to build, test, and deploy agents on Azure infrastructure. Finally, Agent 365 gives IT teams a place to see which agents are running, monitor their activity, and set policies.

Customer stories will also be a big part of each of the four innovation sessions.

Where should your AI actually run? Mark Russinovich and Pavan Davuluri will lead “AI Infrastructure From Cloud to Edge,” with examples of Microsoft using its own tech as “Customer Zero” (what Microsoft calls its high-stakes version of dogfooding). PricewaterhouseCoopers will appear in person, and OpenAI, Adobe, and Replit will share featured videos in this session. If you’re deciding what to run in Azure vs. closer to users, this session will offer the insight you need.

Microsoft reports that more than 40,000 people at Lilly use Copilot

How do you get people using agents in their everyday work? Lilly’s Bryce Williams is scheduled to join Microsoft’s Jacob Andreou in person for “Expanding What’s Possible: How AI Is Redesigning Work.” Microsoft reports that more than 40,000 people at Lilly use Copilot, and that more than 150 agents support work across research, clinical trials, and operations. If your team is rolling out Copilot, Lilly will showcase what helped its teams adopt it at scale.

How do you ensure your agents are working from the right information? In “Harnessing Your IQ With a Continuously Improving Agent Platform,” Arun Ulag and Jay Parikh will look at how agents use company data and knowledge, with planned spotlights on AEMO and NTT Data. You’ll hear how teams decide what an agent should be able to see and how they test whether it’s drawing on the right information.

How will you know your agents are working once they’re rolled out? Charles Lamanna and Hayete Gallot will lead “Observability at Every Layer for Every Role,” with planned videos from Royal Philips and KPMG, plus an onstage interview with the Bank of England. The Bank says nearly all of its employees use Microsoft 365 Copilot each week. Some agents that started as experiments are now in wider use, including one that answers staff questions about leave and pay. If you’re curious how to tell when an agentic system is trusted and ready for prime time, you’ll find out here.

Between sessions, you can explore demonstrations in Moscone South, where planned customer installations include Alaska Airlines, Unilever, and more, with technical experts on hand. Theater sessions and lightning talks will also offer more time for questions.

There’s also a reason to step outside onto Howard Street between Third and Fourth streets, where plans include NFL and Premier League installations and a Mercedes-AMG PETRONAS Formula One car display.

If you’re heading to San Francisco, there’s still time to register for Microsoft Ignite and browse the session catalog. If you’re following from home, you can use the same registration page to get a free digital pass.

How to watch Microsoft Ignite 2026

Tune in to Live at Microsoft Ignite at 10 a.m. Pacific (1 p.m. Eastern) on Tuesday, November 17, to watch the opening keynote from Nadella and Althoff in full. The broadcast continues over the next three days with demos, customer stories, and executive interviews. The New Stack ‘s own Jennifer Riggins will join the anchor desk throughout the show to talk through what the announcements mean for teams building and running AI in production.

Alysa Taylor, Microsoft’s Commercial Chief Marketing Officer, says to “Come with a challenge you’re excited to solve, whether that’s bringing ambition into the flow of work, connecting intelligence across your organization with the right data and context, or scaling AI innovation to drive meaningful business impact.

“Take in what you see on stage, then go deeper with the builders, customers, and leaders who are working through these same opportunities. The real value is connecting inspiration to action, and leaving with ideas you can put to work.”

Leave some time for networking after your sessions, too. If someone just described an agent you could imagine running in your organization, ask what it costs to scale, which metrics they are watching, or how they got their colleagues to adopt it.

articles.title: Corsair HX1000i Shift Crystal power supply review: 1000W Platinum efficiency with an eye-catching transparent aesthetic
articles.description: Corsair puts the internals of a CWT-built, Cybenetics Platinum 1000W platform on display behind three clear panels, adding side-mounted connectors, iCUE LINK integration and per-pin 12V-2x6 protection.
articles.content:
Corsair needs very little introduction to anyone who has built a PC over the past two decades. Founded in California in 1994 as a manufacturer of memory modules, the company has since grown into one of the largest brands in the PC component and peripheral market, with a catalog that covers cases, cooling, keyboards, mice, streaming gear, and of course, power supplies. Corsair entered the PSU market in the second half of the 2000s and built its reputation there by choosing its OEM partners carefully rather than manufacturing in-house. Channel Well Technology (CWT) has been one of the most important of these partners, producing a large portion of the RMx and HXi units over the years. The HXi series in particular has long been Corsair's high-end, digitally monitored family, positioned just below the flagship AX models.

We take a closer look at the HX1000i Shift Crystal to see if it deserves a spot in our best power supplies list. The HX1000i Shift Crystal is a bit of an odd bird, and Corsair is clearly fine with that. First shown at Computex 2026 and launching on November 12th, it combines the side-mounted connector layout of the SHIFT models with the digital HXi platform, and then wraps everything in a chassis with clear polycarbonate panels on three sides, turning the internals of the PSU into a part of the build's aesthetics. Beneath the show, the platform is built by CWT. It holds a Cybenetics Platinum certification at both 115 VAC and 230 VAC, and it is fully compliant with the ATX 3.1 and PCIe 5.1 design guides. It also integrates an iCUE LINK System Hub and Corsair's PinProtect+ per-pin current monitoring for the native 12V-2x6 connector. The 1000W model that we are reviewing today is rated to deliver its full power output continuously at ambient temperatures up to 50°C and comes with a ten-year warranty.

In the Box

The HX1000i Shift Crystal ships in a very large and sturdy black cardboard box, with a large render of the unit on the front that does a good job of showing off the transparent panels and the lit fan. The model name is printed in big yellow and white letters across the bottom half, while the badges in the top right corner - ATX 3.1 with PCIe 5.1 and 12V-2x6 support, the Cybenetics certifications, and the iCUE LINK logo- tell you most of what you need to know before even opening the package.

(Image credit: Tom's Hardware) The bundle is rather spartan for a product of this class. Inside the box, we found the AC power cord, four mounting screws, a handful of black cable ties, and a leaflet with safety and compliance information. There are no Velcro straps, no cable combs beyond those already on the cables, and no other accessories of any kind. It is not a deal breaker by any means, but a premium unit like this that is focused on aesthetics could have been a little more generous in this department.

(Image credit: Tom's Hardware) All of the cables are fully modular and black, with individually sleeved wires and low-profile cable combs. There is a 24-pin ATX cable, two 4+4-pin EPS cables, three PCIe cables carrying four 6+2-pin connectors in total, and a native 12V-2x6 cable rated for 600W, alongside two SATA and two Molex cables with four connectors each. Eight Molex connectors on a modern 1000W unit is extremely generous, frankly more than any reasonable build will ever need. Corsair also supplies two iCUE LINK cables of different lengths and a USB cable that connects the PSU's monitoring interface to the motherboard.

External Appearance

With dimensions of 150 x 86 x 200 mm, the HX1000i Shift Crystal is a long ATX unit, which is a non-issue if you are getting the matching Corsair 4500X case anyway. In any other case, you will need to check your case's specifications before buying one. The side-mounted SHIFT connectors also require some free space next to the PSU, as the cables plug into the side of the unit instead of its face, which is great for cases with a hidden PSU compartment but not suitable for every chassis. The design is unlike anything else on the market. The steel frame is black, with Y-shaped cutouts forming the fan grille and a debossed pattern of the same shape on the opposite panel, while three of the sides are clear polycarbonate panels that reveal the white fan frame, the bulk capacitors, the coils, and the white PCBs. With the RGB fan lit, the unit very much looks like a piece of display hardware rather than a power supply.

(Image credit: Tom's Hardware) The rear of the unit is a little more conventional, with the AC receptacle, a rocker on/off switch marked with the "HX1000i SHIFT" logo, and a large perforated area with the same Y-shaped cutouts for the exhaust. The modular connector bay is on the side, behind the clear panel. The face opposite the AC receptacle hosts the white control PCB, also visible through its clear panel, with two iCUE LINK ports, a USB Type-C port, and a small port marked "TACH". The hexagonal specifications sticker is on the solid steel top side of the unit and is an envelope-type that can be closed to hide the text.

Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware The CRYSTAL is fully compatible with Corsair's iCUE software, which can be used to monitor the PSU, adjust its fan speed, and switch the 12V overcurrent protection between single- and multi-rail modes. Corsair also integrated an iCUE LINK System Hub that, according to the company, supports up to 24 iCUE LINK devices without the need for a separate hub. The most interesting addition, however, is PinProtect+, Corsair's per-pin current monitoring for the 12V-2x6 connector. If the current on a pin exceeds a user-customizable threshold, the PSU cuts power to the connector, and the RGB fan lighting turns red to signal the fault. Given the history of melting connectors, this is a genuinely useful feature rather than marketing fluff. We can confirm that it is working as intended, as we tried pulling 20A from a single wire of the 12V-2x6 connector and the PSU shut down instantly.

Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware Internal Design

Cooling is handled by a 140 mm Corsair NR140HL-RGB fan. Corsair calls it a magnetic dome bearing design, and in practice it is a rifle-bearing fan with a half-domed shaft magnet, rated at 0.55A on 12V. The fan is white with addressable lighting, which also doubles as the visual alarm for PinProtect+. It is a decent fan, and the magnetic shaft should help with longevity, but it is worth mentioning that the regular HX1000i SHIFT uses a fluid dynamic bearing fan, which we would normally consider the better choice for a premium unit.

(Image credit: Tom's Hardware) The OEM behind the HX1000i Shift Crystal is Channel Well Technology (CWT), Corsair's long-time partner for its HXi units. Almost every part inside the unit has been relabeled as "Corsair", including the capacitors and the magnetic components, so the OEM is not obvious at a glance, but the Cybenetics report confirms it. The layout is extremely clean and obviously optimized for aesthetics, which also explains the excessive length of the chassis. The bridge rectifiers have their own heatsink, the APFC components sit on another large heatsink, and the primary switchers have their own heatsink as well, while the secondary side components are on a vertical PCB right after the main transformer. All heatsinks are of good size and quality.

Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware The transient filtering stage has four Y capacitors, three X capacitors, and two filtering inductors. Two bridge rectifiers sharing a large heatsink feed the APFC stage, which relies on two Infineon 60R099P6 MOSFETs and two fully encased filtering coils. The APFC stage also includes two bulk capacitors, one Corsair 560 μF / 420 V capacitor and one Corsair 470 μF / 420 V capacitor, for a combined capacity of 1030 μF. According to the Cybenetics report, these capacitors are supplied by Elite, a relatively reputable Taiwanese manufacturer, and they are rated for 105°C. They are not capacitors that we frequently encounter in anything above mid-tier, though, and we feel they are not a great match for a premium unit.

Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware The primary inversion stage uses two more Infineon 60R099P6 MOSFETs in a half-bridge LLC resonant topology. On the secondary side, ten Infineon 014N04LS MOSFETs handle the synchronous rectification of the 12V rail, and the minor rails are derived from DC-to-DC converters. All of the capacitors on the secondary side are rebranded as Corsair, with black and white sleeves that match the color scheme of the unit, and are also made by Elite. These are mostly good parts, but it is a bit ironic that Corsair advertises 105°C Japanese electrolytic capacitors for the regular HX1000i SHIFT, while the version built to show its capacitors off uses Taiwanese ones.

(Image credit: Tom's Hardware) Cold Test Results (25°C Ambient)

Cold Test Results (25°C Ambient)

For the testing of PSUs, we are using high-precision electronic loads with a maximum power draw of 2700 Watts, a Rigol DS5042M 40 MHz oscilloscope, an Extech 380803 power analyzer, two high-precision UNI-T UT-325 digital thermometers, an Extech HD600 SPL meter, a self-designed hotbox, and various other bits and parts.

Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware At 25°C ambient, the HX1000i Shift Crystal is a very efficient power supply. It averaged 92.1% at 230 VAC and 90.5% at 115 VAC across the nominal load range, with the efficiency peaking at 93.6% (230 VAC) and 92.2% (115 VAC) at around 40% load. The curve is relatively flat after that, with the unit still achieving 91% at 230 VAC and 88.5% at 115 VAC while delivering its full 1000W. The efficiency at very low loads is good as well, at just over 88% with a 50W load on 230 VAC. These figures are in line with the unit's Cybenetics Platinum certification at both input voltages. There is no 80 PLUS certification for this unit.

The acoustics at room temperature are very good. The fan stays completely off up to 50% load, so a typical gaming system with a powerful graphics card will rarely ever wake it up. Once it starts, the unit registers 31.6 dB(A) at 500W, and the fan ramps up very gently, staying around 33 dB(A) at 700W and below 37 dB(A) at 900W. Only at full load does the noise climb to about 39 dB(A), which is still a low figure for a 1000W unit. Thermal performance gives no reason for concern at all, with the primary and secondary heatsinks reaching just 55°C and 58°C respectively at full load.

Hot Test Results (~45°C Ambient)

Hot Test Results (~45°C Ambient)

Inside our hotbox, at roughly 45°C ambient and still within the unit's 50°C rating, the HX1000i Shift Crystal hardly lost any efficiency at all. It averaged 91.7% at 230 VAC and 90.1% at 115 VAC, a drop of just 0.4 percentage points compared to the cold test. The peak efficiency dropped to 93.3% and 91.9%, respectively, and the full-load efficiency to 90.6% and 88.1%. That is a very strong result that shows how well the platform tolerates high ambient temperatures.

articles.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns in the wake of multiple affairs, Chinese spy allegations
articles.description: NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) Board of Directors announced today that Jensen Huang has resigned as President, Chief Executive Officer, and a member of the Board, effective immediately.
articles.content:
Nvidia’s board of directors has confirmed today that Jensen Huang has resigned as the company's CEO. The news follows revelations that Huang had been involved in not one but two extramarital affairs, one with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset, and another with his direct report, Nvidia’s VP of health care, Kimberly Powell.

"NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) Board of Directors announced today that Jensen Huang has resigned as President, Chief Executive Officer, and a member of the Board, effective immediately," the board stated. "Colette Kress, current Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer of NVIDIA, has agreed to serve as Interim Chief Executive Officer. Kress will continue to serve as Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer while serving as Interim Chief Executive Officer until a permanent successor has been named. The Board is initiating a search for a permanent Chief Executive Officer and will consider internal and external candidates."

In recent weeks, stories have come to light alleging that Huang was involved in an overly familiar relationship with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom U.S. intelligence agencies suspect may be a Chinese intelligence asset. It was reported that the AI GPU giant’s CEO may have been the target of a spy plot — Megaspeed is under investigatio n for its involvement in the smuggling of $2 billion worth of export-controlled AI GPUs into China.

Nvidia shares plunged more than 10 percent in early market trading following the news, and are now down more than 23% in the last month.

Over the weekend, Jensen Huang admitted that he had been unfaithful to his wife and issued a company-wide apology. Separately, Nvidia’s Board of Directors launched an independent investigation into reports that Huang’s entanglement may be a matter of national security, given his role in the global AI revolution.

Colette Kress has been Nvidia's Executive Vice President and CFO since September 2013; prior to that, she spent 25 years at Cisco and Microsoft, among others.

Just a couple of days later, a second bombshell report emerged claiming that Jensen Huang was also romantically involved with Powell, one of his direct reports at the company. Reports indicate the affair was known within the company, and that the two were even filmed being affectionate in a San Jose hotel at Nvidia GTC. Security allegedly sequestered a bystander who filmed the interaction on camera and made the person an offer to sign a nondisclosure agreement.

Nvidia also announced that Harvey C. Jones will serve as the company's first-ever Chair of the Board; he has previously served as CEO and Executive Chairman of Synopsys.

articles.title: Quantum leap: IBM plans to scale beyond 1,000 qubits in 2027 with Nighthawk r3 processor
articles.description: New unit sports more qubits and is planned to be part of future fault-tolerant rig
articles.content:
IBM has unveiled the Nighthawk r3, an upcoming next-gen quantum processor that will feature 520 qubits, as another step towards a planned fault-tolerant quantum system it hopes to launch in 2029.

Big Blue's current Nighthawk r2 was only made available in September and features 120 quantum bits (qubits) capable of handling circuits using 7,500 operations.

Its successor, IBM claims, will have more than four times as many qubits and execute 10,000 quantum operations to tackle larger, more complex problems while maintaining the same speed and accuracy.

Nighthawk r3 is slated to arrive in 2027, when Big Blue plans to link two of the quantum processors into a single system with more than 1,000 qubits.

IBM said applications increasingly require circuits executing thousands of quantum operations on approximately 100 qubits or more, speeding up collection of the millions or billions of samples needed to perform complex computations. Speed determines whether such demanding workloads can be completed in practical timeframes and at a reasonable cost.

The new quantum processor will feature 10 chip-to-chip interconnects, called l-couplers, designed for linking together processors that it will use to enable a single 1,040-qubit system. This tech was tested using Nighthawk r1 processors.

IBM previously outlined its goal of reaching reliable error correcting territory in 2029 with a quantum processor codenamed Starling. Now it intends for this to be the world’s first fault-tolerant quantum computer, capable of running quantum circuits comprising 100 million quantum operations on 200 logical qubits.

This is an ambitious goal, considering fault-tolerant quantum technology always seems to be at least a decade away, despite numerous breakthroughs and technology introductions. However, some in the technology industry believe the odds on a working system are shortening, given the increased activity around making encryption ready with support for quantum-resistant algorithms.

Then again, a professor at the University of Auckland New Zealand famously claimed last year that quantum computers hadn't so far managed to factor any number greater than 21 without cheating.

IBM presented a framework for Starling in a 2025 paper outlining hardware to implement the improbably named bivariate bicycle quantum low-density parity check (qLDPC) error correction codes. These significantly reduce the number of physical qubits needed to store and process quantum information, compared to existing surface codes.

Using the architecture in the paper, Big Blue intends to assemble Starling from modules that each contain a quantum memory and logical processing unit (LPU), allowing logic operations on the memory. The modules will have universal adapters letting them connect using l-couplers.

IBM is also preparing the way ahead by combining its quantum processors with classical high-performance compute (HPC) systems to research better quantum error correction.

Last week, Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) in the US announced such a system, combining an IBM Quantum System Two with Nighthawk r2 quantum processors and Umbra, powered by AMD 5th Gen Epyc CPUs and Instinct MI355X GPU accelerators.

IBM also has a partnership with Japan's RIKEN scientific research institute under which an IBM Quantum System Two has been integrated with the Fugaku Arm-based supercomputer, once the most powerful system in the world. ®

NASA’s Hubble Offers Cosmic Sampler of Targets for Roman

A collage of strong gravitational lenses observed by Hubble, some of which will be followed up by observations with the Roman Space Telescope, which launched in August 2026. Lenses like these will be used to investigate the evolution of galaxies and dark matter.

Credit: NASA, ESA, and X. Huang (University of San Francisco); Processing: Gladys Kober (NASA/Catholic University of America)

A gallery of gravitational lenses captured by NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope showcases the diversity of this cosmic phenomenon and lays the groundwork for follow-up observations by the new Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope.

Gravitational lensing, first predicted by Albert Einstein, occurs when the gravity of a massive foreground object, such as a galaxy or cluster of galaxies, bends, warps, and magnifies the light from a more distant background object. The effect is similar to that of a giant lens in space that allows astronomers to view objects much farther away than any telescope could see on its own.

The lenses in this image formed from the precise alignment of a distant background galaxy with the mass of a foreground galaxy, creating distorted and magnified images of the background galaxy that appear as arcs around the foreground galaxy.

Astronomers will use these observations of a large and varied population of gravitational lenses to construct lens models that will help determine how much mass is in the lensing system’s foreground galaxy – and potentially prove or dispel a theory about dark matter. Astronomers study the amount of distortion of the lensed background galaxies to determine the quantity and distribution of mass in the foreground galaxy, including its invisible dark matter.

Hubble views the cosmos primarily in visible and ultraviolet light with some infrared coverage, providing a comprehensive, high-resolution view of individual objects. Roman sees primarily infrared light and some visible, over a much larger field of view to create panoramas of the universe. While Hubble gets a better view of individual lenses, Roman will be able to capture more lenses with its wider field-of-view. If Roman finds a particularly interesting lens, researchers may use Hubble to take follow-up observations using its visible and UV prowess for individual objects.

With Hubble’s high-resolution imaging and precise models, researchers should also be able to detect small imperfections in these gravitationally lensed galaxy arcs that would indicate the presence of small clumps of dark matter. Researchers could use these previously undetected clumps to confirm the cold dark matter theory, which predicts the existence of many small dark matter clumps of between a million to a billion solar masses. In contrast, the dark matter halo of our Milky Way galaxy is around 1.3 trillion solar masses.

By studying Hubble lens images in detail, researchers intend to build a super-intelligence tool to efficiently search similar arcs in the upcoming Roman images. The Hubble images are expected to both yield their own results on dark matter and pave the way for analysis of Roman’s larger sample of lenses.

The unique lenses in this image display some of the different characteristics researchers will see as they collect a diverse and numerous assortment of lenses to test in their models. Panel A is an example of an arc-counterarc configuration, in which the lensed background galaxy appears as a duplicated pair of arcs. The lensed galaxy is being magnified by a pair of foreground galaxies whose combined mass bends the light of the background galaxy around them.

The diversity of lenses in this image demonstrate some of the characteristics researchers will uncover with Hubble and Roman. Each lens differs significantly from others in the panel.

Credit: NASA, ESA, and X. Huang (University of San Francisco); Processing: Gladys Kober (NASA/Catholic University of America)

Panel F is an Einstein Ring, in which the alignment of the background galaxy and approximately spherical mass of the foreground lens are so perfectly situated that the lensed galaxy almost fully encircles the foreground galaxy. Panel I shows a quadruply lensed galaxy, in which the background galaxy is replicated four times, appearing as smeared dots around the foreground galaxy. Panel C also shows a quadruply lensed galaxy, with double knots that are most likely strong star-forming regions in the background galaxy.

Some of the magnified and warped background galaxies appear blue and some appear red. These bluish arcs indicate young stars, while reddish arcs indicate older stars. Roman and Hubble will explore these differences to better understand how galaxies evolved earlier in the universe.

Most of the foreground lensing galaxies are elliptical galaxies, which are older, denser, and more compact. Lensed images of background galaxies only occur when the mass density of the foreground galaxy reaches a critical point.

But not all of these foreground galaxies are ellipticals, and researchers can use these differences to explore the evolutionary paths taken by these galaxies. In panel G, the foreground galaxy appears elongated, which may be true or a trick of perspective, and in panels B and F, the foreground galaxies appear to have spiral arms.

Panel D’s foreground galaxy has a visible dust lane, which is rare in a lensing galaxy and the kind of detail that Hubble’s sharp, visible-light vision excels at revealing. The lensed background galaxy could be an Einstein Ring, with the dust lane “breaking” our view of the ring. Because infrared light is less obscured by dust, future Roman infrared observations could help determine whether the arcs form a more complete Einstein ring.

These strong lenses were first detected with The Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument at Kitt Peak. Hubble subsequently observed them, and Roman will take further observations. Images like these are an example of the kinds of collaborative efforts that routinely take place between NASA’s Great Observatories to build a comprehensive picture of the cosmos. As Roman joins the family of large space observatories that includes Hubble, the Chandra X-ray Observatory, and the James Webb Space Telescope, a new window opens onto the universe, revealing sights previously hidden while expanding our cosmic knowledge for all of humanity.

This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.

What to know about this year’s UN climate talks

Thousands of delegates, lobbyists, and journalists have gathered in Antalya, Turkey, for COP31, the annual UN climate talks. But this year’s negotiations are taking place against a particularly tense geopolitical backdrop, as the world falls further behind the Paris Agreement’s goals.

Energy prices are soaring, and there are big questions about how countries will tackle the climate crisis. Expect a lot of back and forth on fossil fuels and climate finance, and whether negotiators can agree on meaningful action.

Here’s what you need to know about COP31. 

—Casey Crownhart

This story is from The Spark, our weekly climate tech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Wednesday.

Inside the quest for cognitive immortality

Far-thinking technologists are working on ways to keep your brain going beyond death. MIT Technology Review’s latest Roundtables event explores their ideas, from gradual brain replacement to uploading memories to the cloud.

Join science editor Mary Beth Griggs and senior editor for biomedicine Antonio Regalado for this subscriber-only discussion.

Tune in live on Tuesday, November 17 at 5:00 p.m. GMT / 12:00 p.m. EST / 9:00 a.m. PST.

Want to join the conversation? Subscribe to MIT Technology Review for exclusive access to all our Roundtables.

The must-reads

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

1 Nvidia is reportedly preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang
The board will meet as soon as today to determine his future. ( WSJ $)
+ Nvidia’s stock slid 8% after the report was published. ( BI )
+ Huang allegedly also had an affair with an Nvidia colleague. ( NYT $)
+ His exit could send shockwaves across the AI industry. ( Axios )
+ Stakes are high in AI’s trillion-dollar gamble. ( MIT Technology Review )

But Commerce Secretary Lutnick has stalled the curbs. ( CNBC )
+ China has signaled it will retaliate if they pass. ( FT $)
+ Chinese firms have started stockpiling Nvidia chips. ( Reuters $)
+ Democrats appear to be preparing an investigation. ( Politico )

3 A startup has built an AI to detect AI-made bioweapons
It runs offline on a laptop with a USB gene sequencer. ( Wired $)
+ Ukraine is opening up its battlefield data to train AI weapons. ( NYT $)
+ AI is making bioweapons easier to create. ( MIT Technology Review )

4 Anduril says its satellite can track spacecraft in orbital night
It uses an infrared sensor to detect hidden satellites. ( Ars Technica )
+ Anduril is also making smart glasses for warfare. ( MIT Technology Review )

5 Ukraine has reported new restrictions on SpaceX’s Starshield
Zelenskyy says they’re hampering drone defenses. ( NBC News

6 Even remote Brazilian wildlife has microplastics in its blood
Animals 100 km from waste sites carried them. ( Nature )
+ AstroTurf is increasing microplastic levels. ( MIT Technology Review )

7 A NASA space camera can spot invasive plants from orbit
It detects how different species’ leaves reflect light. ( Economist $)

8 Astronomers have found an “invisible” object that defies stellar theory
It’s likely an ultra-rare supermassive neutron star. ( 404 Media )

9 Life may have started with metabolism, not genes
Self-sustaining chemical cycles could have come first. ( Quanta )

10 Brain surgery has left a man seeing cat eyes on people
Researchers used AI to render what he sees. ( Gizmodo )

China’s short drama industry is fueled by bite-sized, melodramatic, and smutty shows built for smartphone scrolling. Now, many are being made entirely with AI: no actors, camera operators, cinematographers, or CGI specialists required.

An average of 470 AI-generated short dramas were released every day in January. Production timelines have shrunk from months to weeks, while costs have dropped by up to 90%. Storytelling is also increasingly driven by performance data.

The format is rapidly expanding overseas while reshaping the work of writers and production crews. Read the full story on AI’s dramatic impact on China’s short drama industry.

articles.title: Noctua brings space-grade carbon nanotube thermal pad to AMD AM5 and AM4 processors
articles.description: Noctua says the NT-CP1 uses carbon nanotubes originally developed for aerospace applications, with the material gradually adapting to microscopic surface imperfections to improve heat transfer over repeated heating and cooling cycles.
articles.content:
Austrian cooling outfit Noctua is officially rolling its new NT-CP1 AM5/4 Carbice carbon nanotube thermal pad for AMD AM4 and AM5 processors into the retail market. After announcing its partnership with advanced nanotechnology company Carbice back in June 2026, the premium thermal pad can now be purchased for $24.95 in the US and €24.95 in the European region.

Grab the Noctua NT-CP1 AM5/4 Carbice carbon nanotube thermal pad on Amazon

Conventional thermal pastes and most thermal pads gradually lose performance over time due to pump-out, delamination, cracking, and other forms of degradation. However, Noctua says that its new NT-CP1 thermal pad takes a different approach. It makes use of Carbice's vertically-aligned carbon nanotube technology, originally developed for high thermal reliability in aerospace systems. The carbon nanotubes gradually conform to microscopic imperfections of a CPU’s IHS over hundreds to thousands of thermal cycles.

This allows heat transfer performance to improve during the initial activation period rather than gradually deteriorating. The thermal pad can also maintain stable, maintenance-free performance for years once the initial activation phase is complete. Thus, making it a suitable option for users who want consistent thermal performance without having to periodically replace degraded thermal paste.

"Carbice pads offer a unique combination of ultimate performance stability and convenient installation. This makes the NT-CP1 the perfect choice for everyone who’s looking for a thermal pad that’s super easy to apply and never needs to be replaced," said Noctua CEO Roland Mossig in a press note.

Unlike conventional carbon or graphite-based thermal pads, which can be brittle, slippery, and electrically conductive, the NT-CP1 features an aluminum backbone sandwiched between layers of carbon nanotubes. The surface is also protected by a nanoscale polymer coating, which Noctua says makes the pad more robust, easier to handle, and less likely to move during installation. The company recommends a simple peel, press, and peel installation process, while the slightly tacky coating helps keep the pad in place and offers electrical insulation as long as the polymer layer remains intact.

With an ultra-thin 90µm profile and precut 33x33mm size, the thermal pad fits both AM5 and AM4 socket processors. Noctua also highlights its manufacturing process, noting that the pad is produced in the US using recycled aluminum and waste carbon gas to grow the carbon nanotubes. The company claims that its manufacturing process is more energy-efficient compared to conventional graphite and graphene-based pads, while the aluminum structure allows the product to be recycled through standard aluminum recycling channels.

articles.title: Hackers exploiting ScreenConnect plugin flaw to spread malware across hundreds of PCs
articles.description: ConnectWise disables third-party extensions in 400 environments as bughunters uncover auth hole may let crims bypass MFA
articles.content:
Hackers have used a dodgy third-party ScreenConnect extension to push malware onto at least 288 machines across 48 organizations, prompting ConnectWise to disable a handful of plugins in hundreds of customer environments.

Security outfit Huntress first raised the alarm in a Reddit post on Wednesday, warning of an active campaign targeting cloud-hosted ScreenConnect instances. At the time, its security operations center was tracking six compromised managed service providers (MSPs) and more than 286 affected endpoints, with the numbers still climbing.

ConnectWise acquired popular remote supporttool ScreenConnect in February, 2015.

Huntress spotted the attacks at around 1747 UTC, when someone began using ScreenConnect's remote command feature to install rogue clients on machines managed by multiple IT service providers. All 288 endpoints were hit within 90 minutes, with roughly a third compromised in the first ten minutes.

Huntress suspects more MSPs may have been compromised, as the attackers appeared to be numbering their victims sequentially, with the numbers suggesting earlier attacks that it hadn't detected.

The attackers deployed a 16-file malware toolkit dubbed SCKit, which installs a separate ScreenConnect client to maintain remote access even if the legitimate connection is shut down. It also contains code designed to spread the infection to IT technicians and potentially other customers under their control.

Huntress has since traced the activity to a possible authentication weakness in RMM+, a third-party extension that lets other management tools issue commands through ScreenConnect without technicians using its console.

Versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32 of the extension contain a flaw that means installations without a configured access key will accept a blank one. Because RMM+ operates independently of ScreenConnect's normal user accounts and authentication controls, an attacker could potentially execute commands without defeating MFA.

Huntress said the findings matched what its investigators saw during the attacks, with commands reaching machines across several ScreenConnect installations despite no corresponding login activity.

The researchers also confirmed that the attacks affected ScreenConnect versions 26.6.6.9747 and 26.7.6.9783, meaning administrators running the latest releases weren't necessarily safe.

ConnectWise has acknowledged that third-party extensions may have been involved but has stopped short of confirming how the attackers initially gained access.

In a security advisory, the company said it was investigating unauthorized access to certain partner environments and had identified approximately 400 installations containing at least one extension from the RMM+ family.

It has disabled five extensions, including RMM+, RMM Plus, and Labtech Plus, wherever it can do so remotely, and urged customers running their own ScreenConnect servers to follow suit.

ConnectWise stressed that the 400 environments were identified because they had the extensions installed, not because they were necessarily compromised.

The company said: "At this time, we have found no evidence of a compromise of ConnectWise infrastructure or a vulnerability in ScreenConnect itself."

There's another nasty trick buried in SCKit. According to Huntress, the malware is designed to turn an infected computer into a trap for the technician sent to investigate it. If the technician connects through ScreenConnect, the toolkit attempts to transfer malware back to their workstation, steal authentication cookies, and use their access to infect other machines.

That could give attackers a route from one compromised customer into others managed by the same IT provider. However, Huntress says it has yet to see that part of the attack succeed.

"We have not observed that method to spread work successfully. The console-takeover attempt failed in every recovered host log we have checked so far," the researchers wrote.

Huntress also suspects that some of the malware's C# code was generated using an LLM, pointing to unusually detailed comments explaining what the code is supposed to do. Apparently, even malware authors appreciate a little help with their homework.

Both Huntress and ConnectWise are urging administrators not to investigate suspected infections by remotely connecting through ScreenConnect, since doing so could put the technician's own machine at risk.

Administrators are being advised to use other security tools to investigate affected machines, look for rogue ScreenConnect clients, and check what commands have been run. Any malware left behind will also need to be removed before the machines are brought back online.

Huntress warned on Reddit that some machines were becoming reinfected within minutes of being taken out of isolation because the malware had not been properly removed.

Simply disabling the vulnerable extensions won't necessarily undo the damage, either. As ConnectWise warns, "Disabling extensions and resetting credentials alone may not remove unauthorized software, persistence mechanisms, or access already established on endpoints."

And with the attackers already able to install their own remote access software, kicking them out could prove considerably harder than closing the door they came through. ®

articles.description: As a new exhibit opens showcasing NASA’s space shuttle Endeavour, NASA photographers look back at the final mission. articles.content:
3 Min Read

Through NASA’s Lens: Capturing Space Shuttle Endeavour’s Move to LA

A spectacular sight as NASA’s Shuttle Carrier Aircraft with space shuttle Endeavour atop soars over the Golden Gate Bridge.

Credits:
NASA/Carla Thomas

As a new exhibit opens showcasing NASA’s space shuttle Endeavour, NASA photographers look back at the final mission. These photographers documented the iconic images shared around the world on Sept. 21, 2012, while millions watched space shuttle Endeavour fly on top of the agency’s 747 Shuttle Carrier Aircraft for the last time.

Endeavour’s new home at the California Science Center in Los Angeles will reopen the weekend of Nov. 13, displayed upright in launch position, ready to inspire the next generation of space explorers.

NASA/Lori Losey

“Chasing Endeavour’s final ferry flight over Southern California was, without a doubt, a leading highlight of my 37-year career at NASA,” said Lori Losey, lead videographer at NASA’s Armstrong Flight Research Center in Edwards, California. “I advocated for two chase aircraft to be used in the LA area so we could dedicate one aircraft to photo and one to video. It was this beautiful dance of alternating altitudes and swapping positions between landmarks to maximize both of us capturing the legendary imagery.”

Two photographers and one videographer, all based at NASA Armstrong, had a leading hand in preparing the Endeavour’s flight to Los Angeles, and in deciding where else the aircraft would fly around California on its final journey. Agency pilots planned the route to fly across some of California’s most iconic landmarks and the imagery team strategized about how to best capture the images.

Thousands of visitors to Disneyland and Disney’s California Adventure parks got a special treat when NASA’s Shuttle Carrier Aircraft with space shuttle Endeavour on top flew over at low level during its flyover of Los Angeles.

NASA/Jim Ross

“The most fun thing about this project was seeing the excitement of the people on the ground as we flew over the different landmarks,” said Jim Ross, NASA Armstrong’s lead photographer. “People in the Los Angeles area really came out and supported the Endeavour flyover. We saw so many supporters at Griffith Park and Disneyland.”

Photographer Carla Thomas said seeing the standing-room-only crowd below the California State Capitol in Sacramento filled her with pride. After joining the agency in the wake of the Challenger tragedy, she reflected on the opportunity to document NASA’s return to flight.

The space shuttle Endeavour and its 747 carrier aircraft makes a low-level flyover of the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum.

NASA/Jim Ross

Endeavour was escorted by NASA Armstrong’s F/A-18s and an F-15, which carried the photo and video teams in the back seats. Like many flight efforts, this journey took a significant amount of preplanning with the California Science Center, as well as groups like the Federal Aviation Administration, the Los Angeles International Airport, and NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston.

“The planning was my favorite part of this effort — it was fun and exciting to plan the shots,” Thomas said. “I flew the entire route with the LAPD (Los Angeles Police Department) in one of their helicopters. We had to make sure this was going to work and find any obstacles. Planning for the Hollywood sign was challenging, because it’s on the side of a hill with power lines and radio antennas, but we worked through these issues in the planning process.”

Space shuttle Endeavour atop its modified 747 carrier aircraft overflies the former Alameda Naval Air Station adjoining San Francisco Bay during the Tour of California.

NASA/Carla Thomas

The space shuttle’s flight path included other California landmarks: Dodger Stadium, the Getty Center, the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum, NASA’s Ames Research Center in Silicon Valley, the Golden Gate Bridge, NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, and the Santa Monica Pier.

Endeavour helped begin assembly of the International Space Station by delivering its first components to orbit and went on to complete 25 missions. The space shuttle will soon be seen, along with some of the images from the final flight, in its permanent home inside the new Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center at the California Science Center in Downtown Los Angeles.

Shuttle Endeavour was ferried to Los Angeles, briefly flying over the California state capitol, Sacramento, then demated from its NASA 747 and trailered to the California Science Center.

NASA/Carla Thomas

articles.title: Suspected Chinese spy at center of Jensen Huang affair surfaces in Beijing
articles.description: There are multiple speculations about Alice Huang's s history and how she built her relationship with Jensen Huang.
articles.content:
Alice Huang, the person allegedly involved in an affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, has reportedly surfaced in Beijing, marking the first sighting of the Megaspeed executive since the scandal broke out. According to Bloomberg, it’s unclear when the suspected Chinese spy arrived in the capital or why she’s in the area, but she was last spotted leaving Singapore for Shanghai in 2025 after she was detained and questioned during the city-state’s investigation into the $2-billion smuggling case involving Megaspeed.

The Nvidia CEO is now under intense scrutiny after the revelation of his indiscretion with the Megaspeed executive, with Congress threatening to issue a subpoena if he does not respond to their invitation to “a joint, closed-door briefing” with the heads of the House committees on China, Foreign Affairs, and Intelligence. The FBI is also looking into the relationship between the head of the largest AI hardware company in the world and a person suspected of helping sanctioned Chinese companies secure hundreds of thousands of banned H100 and H200 chips. Overnight, a second bombshell report claims that Jensen Huang was also involved in an extramarital affair with Nvidia's VP of health care, Kimberly Powell.

Although the Chinese embassy in Washington has denied any links to Alice Huang, calling it nothing but “groundless smears and slanders” against Beijing, there is speculation that she’s under the control of the Ministry of State Security (MSS), which is the primary agency that handles China’s foreign intelligence and counterintelligence operations. The U.S. intelligence community suggests that she may be passing on information to the MSS, but it remains unclear if she was specifically tasked by Chinese intelligence to target Jensen Huang or if they were only leveraging her relationship with the Nvidia chief to get insights into the U.S. AI industry.

A deeper investigation into Alice Huang, known by her Chinese name as Huang Le, revealed that she supposedly worked in media before jumping into banking and finance. The Wall Street Journal reports that it’s unclear when she met her husband, Kang Wei, but the couple ran a private equity and investment management firm called Shanghai Hexi in 2016. This allowed the couple to invest in companies across industries, including gaming, pharmaceuticals, and, eventually, data centers and cloud computing.

The couple is known for riding trends and isn’t a stranger to scandals. Their firm, Shanghai Hexi, invested in gaming companies in the 2010s, especially when mobile gaming started to boom across the world, while Chinese regulators fined Kang and the company in 2018 for disclosure failures and other violations while it was in the midst of a takeover battle for a corporation. Kang’s moves in the gaming industry are what allowed him to meet Jensen Huang, which eventually led to a close relationship between the couple and the Nvidia chief. Sources told the WSJ that Kang apparently accepted Alice and Jensen’s extra-marital relationship, even sometimes jokingly telling people that she was Jensen’s “personal assistant.”

It seems that the couple is used to leveraging their relationships to gain business advantage, and with investments in AI data centers expected to hit $32 trillion by 2050, Alice Huang’s “close” relationship with Jensen Huang put Shanghai Hexi in an excellent position to take advantage of the trend through Megaspeed and make big money. And with U.S. sanctions making it harder for competitors to acquire Nvidia chips, it appears that their access has turned into a gold mine for the company. But whether Alice Huang acted solely out of business interest with the supposed procurement of Nvidia chips or was leveraged by Chinese authorities to import these chips, the fact remains that $7.5 billion worth of banned chips reportedly made their way into China despite Washington’s efforts.

articles.title: The latest FreeBSD report is here, and the AI debate is ongoing
articles.description: Only a minority want to ban it. Plus plenty of updates on 16 projects
articles.content:
The FreeBSD project's status team has published FreeBSD's third status report of 2026, showing plenty of ambitious work underway and a community still undecided on how to treat code from AI coding assistants.

The FreeBSD Status Report Third Quarter 2026 is a substantial document, with 51 entries from five teams covering 16 projects, plus six other sections with more detailed reports.

There are updates on the progress of the Sylve project, which is an attempt to bring a smooth polished GUI for managing FreeBSD virtualization hosts – something akin to Proxmox for FreeBSD. We mentioned this when we looked at the new Daemonarchy project last month. Another covers the new AppJail effort – a containerized app distribution system for FreeBSD, including for GUI apps, which aims for something broadly comparable to Snap, Flatpak and AppImage on Linux.

In other words, interesting and quite radical stuff is happening in the FreeBSD space.

What this particular LLM-skeptical vulture was most interested to see, though, was an update on the internal discussion about how to handle code generated by AI coding assistants in the project. We first reported on this vexed subject back in September 2025 and no final answer has yet been published.

NetBSD banned AI-generated code in 2024 and although the bot-boosters say this will doom it to irrelevance, as we reported last month, the project is thriving. Also back in October, we looked at OpenBSD 8.0, whose launch materials are full of mockery for AI users.

Under the FreeBSD Core Team section, there is a subsection headed "FreeBSD Developer AI survey." The survey was created by Baptiste Daroussin, and received 140 responses. Although the percentages show that there is some resistance to AI, there are hints here as to why it’s taking so long. Some project committers are against it, yet many more are proponents. Since there are only seven bullet points, we thought we would quote them in full:

Policy: 88 percent want the Project to adopt a policy, either a formal, written policy (49 percent ) or light guidance and best practices (39 percent ). Six percent said that AI should be explicitly discouraged, and three percent that the existing contribution rules are sufficient.

AI-assisted code: 35 percent said it must be disclosed, 25 percent that it must be reviewed more strictly than human code, 22 percent that it should be treated like any other contribution, and 16 percent that it should be rejected outright.

Safeguards: mandatory human review (78 percent ) and mandatory disclosure (69 percent ) were requested most often, followed by provenance or licensing documentation (47 percent ) and mandatory testing (39 percent ).

Disclosure: 84 percent want AI use disclosed, either always (48 percent ) or when its involvement is significant (36 percent ). 79 percent want AI-assisted commits marked in the commit log, and 56 percent prefer a tag that names the tool.

Concerns: the main concerns about quality are correctness and subtle bugs (39 percent, licensing and provenance (26 percent ), and maintainability (21 percent ). 75 percent are somewhat or very concerned about copyright and licensing.

Principles: accountability, meaning that a human remains responsible (91 percent ), and transparency (78 percent ) were selected most often, and preserving code quality was the top-ranked goal for a policy.

Other uses: 65 percent would allow AI-generated documentation with human review. 54 percent would allow AI tools on Project infrastructure, most of them with restrictions, and 29 percent would not.

Only six percent for explicit discouragement, 16 percent for outright rejection, and 35 percent against LLM-generated documentation. This plus the usual sort of calls for responsible use and disclosure, concerns about copyright issues, and so on.

The Reg is strongly reminded of the Debian developer poll we reported on in August. This had no fewer than four slightly different AI-refusal options out of eight, and despite the Condorcet voting method it uses, the result was giving permission to use bots.

With such relatively weak opposition, we suspect that FreeBSD will go the same way as Debian: tell developers to be careful, but allow bot usage, resulting in LLM-extruded code being committed into the project. ®

articles.title: Microsoft admits SQL Servers might wobble after October update
articles.description: Linked server connections can linger long past their welcome
articles.content:
Encountered some odd SQL Server connection behavior since the October update? There might be a culprit… Microsoft has admitted that a change has caused linked server queries to fail to close connections.

Linked servers via OLE DB providers have been around for years and are a useful way of, for example, using additional data sources in queries. Once a provider is added, SQL Server can open a connection to grab data, and close it again when the query is complete. Or, at least, that's the theory.

The problem is that after the October 13 (KB5126646) update, connections created by SQL Server linked server queries might remain open. According to Microsoft, "As additional queries are performed, connections to external databases can accumulate instead of closing as expected.

"This can slow or degrade server performance after prolonged run time."

You think? Administrators will likely have already noted a suspicious number of open connections to external databases on affected systems.

Microsoft said the issue affects SQL Server linked server queries that use OLE DB providers to connect to external databases. It gave PostgreSQL and Oracle as examples of connections known to be affected.

And the fix? "If idle connections can be identified, it is possible to manually close them to temporarily relieve server load.

"It is also possible to temporarily restore system stability by restarting the SQL service."

The Windows behemoth went on to state the obvious: "However, these steps can also interrupt active queries or transactions, and the problem can resurface again after sufficient operation time."

Bouncing a SQL Server to deal with connection leakage is less than ideal, although it would at least be a good failover test and, let's face it, having to restart Microsoft services regularly is something many administrators will be all too familiar with.

There is a mitigation available, although only through Microsoft support for business. Otherwise, an out-of-band update should be along within the next few days to deal with the problem.

According to Microsoft, the technical glitch affects every version of Windows except Windows 11 26H2, stretching back to Windows 10 1809 and LTSC 2019, and Windows Server from 2025 back to 2012.

Microsoft, or rather the unfortunate souls responsible for administering their server products, has not had the best time of late. The October 2026 Windows Server update left some Exchange Servers wobbling until either a Registry edit was made or a fix was applied as part of the November update. ®
